purpose: This exam assesses whether candidates can design LLM-based solutions that meet given requirements, using architecture guidance and operational recommendations in the official documentation of the three providers.
guide:
### 1. Introduction

**Purpose**: This exam assesses whether candidates can design LLM-based solutions that meet given requirements, using architecture guidance and operational recommendations in the official documentation of the three providers.

**Objectives**

- Select models and configurations that simultaneously meet quality, cost, latency, and data protection requirements.
- Design knowledge architectures (long context, managed retrieval, RAG) appropriate to data volume and update frequency.
- Plan capacity with throughput and quotas in mind.
- Design security around retention, regional processing, and safety configuration requirements.
- Design for reliability when models are replaced or retired.

### 2. Target Candidates

- Solutions architects, AI engineers, presales engineers, technical consultants

**Recommended background and exam scope**

- Basic cloud architecture knowledge and 1 year of LLM system design experience are recommended.
- Implementation details and deep multi-agent orchestration are outside scope (covered by AEP).

### 3. Content Domains

| Domain | Weight |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Model and Inference Configuration Selection | 20% |
| 2. Knowledge and Data Architecture | 20% |
| 3. Performance and Cost Design | 22% |
| 4. Security and Data Protection Design | 20% |
| 5. Reliability and Quality Design | 18% |

**Domain 1: Model and Inference Configuration Selection**

- Knowledge: Differences in capability, pricing, and speed between model tiers; reasoning effort settings; context windows and output limits; multimodal support.
- Skills: Route requests to different models based on difficulty; select the least expensive configuration that meets accuracy targets.

**Domain 2: Knowledge and Data Architecture**

- Knowledge: Differences between long-context input, managed file retrieval, custom RAG, and web grounding; retrieval quality techniques such as contextual retrieval.
- Skills: Select a knowledge architecture based on document count, update frequency, and access separation requirements.

**Domain 3: Performance and Cost Design**

- Knowledge: Prompt/context caching, batch processing, rate limits and quotas, Provisioned Throughput, and processing priority tiers.
- Skills: Select capacity and billing options for steady, spiky, or overnight bulk traffic; select configurations that meet latency targets.

**Domain 4: Security and Data Protection Design**

- Knowledge: API data retention and Zero Data Retention (ZDR) options, regional data processing, abuse monitoring, safety settings, and least-privilege tool access.
- Skills: Select configurations that satisfy regulatory requirements such as no retention or processing in a specified region.

**Domain 5: Reliability and Quality Design**

- Knowledge: Evaluation-driven development, hallucination reduction, consistency, model retirement schedules, and fallbacks.
- Skills: Design model-version migration procedures with the lowest regression risk.

questions.title: Starting model and cost-reduction path for an accuracy-first workload
questions.prompt:
A team is building an insurance claims review assistant with the Claude API. It reads claim documents and determines whether payout criteria are violated, so incorrect decisions are costly. The requirements are:

- **Meeting the accuracy target is the top priority** at launch.
- After launch, **cost must decrease gradually** while accuracy is maintained.
- Model selection must be justified by the team's own evaluation results.

Which plan best follows Anthropic's model selection guide?

options.text: Start with cost-sensitive Claude Haiku 5.5, measure accuracy on a task evaluation set, and upgrade only underperforming categories to Opus 5.5 before launch.
Start with Claude Opus 5.5, optimize prompts on the task evaluation set, then lower effort or model tier to reduce cost; consider Fable 5.1 if even high effort is insufficient.
Use the top model, Claude Fable 5.1, for all requests from the outset to ensure accuracy, record evaluation results, and consider savings after reviewing usage one year after launch.
Start with Claude Opus 5.5 and optimize prompts, but downgrade to Sonnet 5.5 immediately before launch without separate evaluation to reduce cost, then monitor and address production errors.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [accuracy target first] and [gradual cost reduction]. Anthropic's model-selection guide offers two starting points. Efficiency-first, starting with Haiku 5.5, suits prototyping, strict latency, cost-sensitive work, and high-volume simple tasks. Performance-first, starting with Opus 5.5, suits accuracy-critical work and complex reasoning. The performance-first path optimizes prompts for Opus 5.5, then reduces effort or model tier for savings, moving to Fable 5.1 only if evaluations remain insufficient at `xhigh` or `max` effort. The guide also says adjusting effort within the same model is often preferable to switching models.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, appropriate for a different situation)**: Recording evaluation evidence is appropriate, but the efficiency-first Haiku 5.5 path starts with simple tasks where latency/cost dominate. High misjudgment costs and [accuracy first at launch] call for the performance-first path.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: It follows the guide's sequence: accuracy-first starting point, evaluation-based optimization, lower effort/model for savings, and the top model only if necessary. The guide uses inadequacy even at `xhigh` or `max` as that threshold.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, overengineered)**: Fable 5.1 costs $10/$50 per MTok input/output, versus Opus 5.5's $4/$20. The guide recommends Fable 5.1 only when high-effort Opus 5.5 is insufficient. Even with evaluation records, using it for everything immediately and postponing savings for a year conflicts with [gradual cost reduction].
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Starting with Opus 5.5 and reducing cost are appropriate, but downgrading without the team's evaluation set violates [model choice grounded in internal evaluation]. Discovering errors after deployment also conflicts with accuracy-first work where misjudgments are costly.

Also note: Default effort varies: Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 use `medium`; Fable 5.1 and Sonnet 5.5 use `high`. Claude 4.7-or-later models return 400 for nondefault `temperature`, `top_p`, or `top_k`, so manage output consistency through prompts and evaluation.

**References**: [Choosing the right model › Choose the best model to start with](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/choosing-a-model) · [Models overview › Compare models](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview) · [Model deprecations › API parameter deprecations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations)

questions.title: Routing traffic containing both simple and complex requests
questions.prompt: About 90% of requests to a customer support platform are inquiry classification and short FAQ responses. The other 10% require comparing information across multiple accounts and constructing multi-step solutions. The architect must design the **least expensive configuration that meets accuracy targets for each request type**. Select **2** designs consistent with provider documentation.

options.text: Use multiple models: a cheaper model handles most requests and escalates only difficult decisions to a more capable model.
Eliminate routing logic and per-route evaluations by sending all requests through one path using the most capable model at maximum reasoning effort.
Choose the default model by context-window size, because a larger window can include more account histories at once and therefore produces more accurate answers.
Evaluate candidate combinations of models and reasoning effort on the same representative production inputs, then choose the lightest setting that exceeds the quality threshold for each route.
Use the highest thinking level even for classification to reduce misclassification.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic describes multi-model strategies pairing an inexpensive model with a top-tier model so most tokens are billed at the lower rate, including an executor-advisor pattern that consults the stronger model for difficult decisions. OpenAI's model selection guide recommends testing models and reasoning effort on the same inputs and retaining the lightest setting that meets the quality threshold. Together, these principles suggest separate routes with evaluations selecting the minimum sufficient configuration for each.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: When most requests are simple, using a cheaper model and escalating only difficult cases can preserve accuracy while reducing cost.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; overengineering)**: Using the highest model tier and effort even for the simple 90% unnecessarily increases latency and output costs, including reasoning tokens.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; confusion between related capabilities)**: A context window measures how many tokens can be referenced at once, not accuracy. Anthropic also warns of context rot: accuracy and recall can fall as token counts grow.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Comparing identical inputs per route and selecting the lightest setting that passes the threshold is the documented way to find the least expensive sufficient configuration.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; overengineering)**: Gemini recommends minimal or low thinking for simple tasks such as factual retrieval and classification. Thinking tokens are billed as output, so maximum thinking increases classification costs unnecessarily.

**References**: [Choosing the right model › Combine models](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/choosing-a-model) · [Model selection › How to think about models and reasoning effort](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-selection) · [Gemini thinking › Best practices](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thinking)

questions.title: Choosing a classification model while accounting for price increases and version policy
questions.prompt:
A pipeline using the Gemini API classifies product reviews as "positive/negative/neutral" using Gemini 3.8 Flash with default settings. Although output is a one-word label, billed output tokens are far higher than expected. The conditions are:

- Reviews must immediately appear in search filters after submission, so processing must remain **synchronous**.
- Company policy allows **only Stable models** in production, and replacements must pass the existing classification evaluation set.
- Labels **must not be truncated or missing**.
- Finance requires **the lowest token unit prices for the 2027 budget**.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Move to Stable Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, set `max_output_tokens` very low to fit the label and reduce thinking tokens, and switch after evaluation passes.
Move to the cheaper Gemini 3 Flash (Preview), explicitly set a low `thinking_level`, and switch after evaluation passes.
Move to Stable Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with explicit low `thinking_level`, collect reviews into Batch API jobs for another 50% discount, and switch after evaluation passes.
Move to Stable Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, explicitly set a low `thinking_level`, and switch after evaluation passes.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [Stable models only] and [minimize unit prices for the 2027 budget]; [no truncation] rules out an easy shortcut. Gemini model documentation describes 3.5 Flash-Lite as the fastest, most cost-efficient Stable 3.5 model for high-throughput tasks. Pricing says Gemini 3.8 Flash input/output prices double to $1.50/$7.50 per 1M from January 1, 2027, while 3.5 Flash-Lite costs $0.30/$2.50. Thinking tokens are billed as output, so a lightweight model with low thinking level and evaluated accuracy offers the greatest unit-cost reduction for simple classification.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: The model and evaluation are appropriate, but `max_output_tokens` includes thinking tokens. Hitting the limit during reasoning yields an "incomplete" response while generated thinking tokens remain billable, violating [no truncation]. Documentation recommends lowering `thinking_level` to reduce cost without cutting off the response.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Gemini 3 Flash is Preview. Despite lower prices, Preview has stricter rate limits and may be discontinued with as little as two weeks' notice, violating [Stable models only].
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: The model, thinking level, and evaluation are suitable; Flash-Lite supports Batch and its 50% discount. But Batch is asynchronous with a 24-hour target, violating [synchronous processing] for immediate search-filter updates after review submission.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It respects Stable policy, lowest unit costs, and evaluation while preserving synchronous calls and reducing output tokens through thinking-level adjustment without truncation risk. Gemini 3.8 Flash doubles in price in 2027 and targets long-running engineering/autonomous agents, making it unsuitable as the lowest-cost simple-classification path.

Also note: If Flash-Lite fails evaluation, lowering `thinking_level` on 3.8 Flash is the fallback. Supported levels vary by model, so verify the target's supported values before switching.

**References**: [Gemini models › Model version name patterns](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/models) · [Gemini API pricing](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing) · [Gemini thinking › Pricing](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thinking) · [Gemini thinking › Best practices](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thinking) · [Batch API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/batch-api) · [Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/models/gemini-3.5-flash-lite)

questions.title: Starting configuration for infrequent overnight decisions based on conflicting evidence
questions.prompt:
You are designing an OpenAI API feature that drafts dispute-response recommendation memos for a legal team. Contracts, emails, and meeting notes frequently assert conflicting facts, so the model must compare contradictory evidence and develop recommendations. The conditions are:

- Jobs run **overnight** 2–3 times per week. The lawyer reviews results the next morning; nobody waits during execution.
- **Output quality is the top priority**, but the budget owner also requires **cost and processing time to be managed**. Cost and latency therefore cannot be ignored.
- After choosing a starting configuration, the team will compare other settings on identical inputs (common to every option).

Which starting configuration best follows OpenAI's model selection guide?

options.text: Start with the strongest model, Astra, at Extra high reasoning effort, then compare quality and cost against lower settings.
Start with the most cost-efficient model, Luna, at Extra high reasoning effort, then compare quality and cost against lower settings.
Start with GPT-6.1 Sol at Extra high reasoning effort, then compare quality and cost against lower settings.
Start with GPT-6.1 Sol at Medium reasoning effort, use its output as a draft requiring lawyer revisions, and compare with higher settings.

questions.explanation:
The decisive facts are [judgment from conflicting evidence], [manage cost and processing time], and [overnight execution]. OpenAI's guide positions GPT-6.1 Sol for complex work that must also manage time and cost, and maps "decisions based on conflicting evidence" to GPT-6.1 Sol at Extra high. It also explains that frequent automation accumulates cost quickly and work with a waiting user needs faster settings. Infrequent overnight execution can accommodate higher effort's time cost, so Sol at Extra high is the appropriate starting point.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, overengineered)**: The guide defaults to Astra when cost and latency are not concerns; this prompt explicitly requires managing both.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, appropriate for a different situation)**: Luna at Extra high is mapped to finding context across apps, prioritizing work, and clearly constrained problems. Judgment from conflicting evidence is outside that category.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: This is the guide's combination for conflicting-evidence decisions. Infrequent overnight execution can tolerate its time cost even while managing cost and processing time.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Sol at Medium is an example for complex technical work where revisions are expected. Overnight execution offers little reason to prioritize speed, and this shifts the quality-first requirement onto human revision.

**References**: [Model selection › Find the right model for your workflow](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-selection) · [Model selection › How to think about models and reasoning effort](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-selection)

questions.title: Combining static manuals with an internal-only inventory API
questions.prompt:
An appliance retailer is building an assistant for store employees using the OpenAI Responses API. The situation and requirements are:

- Around 20,000 product manual PDFs contain hundreds of millions of tokens. Only some change each month. Answers using manuals must **show the source file**.
- Inventory and prices per store **change minute by minute**, and answers must use **values current at the time of the question**.
- The inventory API is accessible only on the internal network. Security policy **does not approve exposing internal systems to the public internet**.
- With only two developers, the team **must not operate its own embedding pipeline or vector database**.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Embed manuals in a custom vector database and return results through a retrieval function tool. Use a separate function tool executed by the app to query the internal inventory API for current inventory/prices.
Put manuals and inventory spreadsheet files in a vector store for `file_search`. Replace inventory files every minute and continuously update the vector store index.
Put manuals in a vector store for `file_search`. Query current inventory/prices using a function tool whose application code calls the internal inventory API and returns results.
Put manuals in a vector store for `file_search`. Expose a remote MCP server wrapping the internal inventory API to the public internet and query inventory/prices through the `mcp` tool.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [values current at question time], [no public internet exposure], and [no self-operated retrieval infrastructure]. All four designs can work technically, but each incorrect option violates one of these constraints. `file_search` is an OpenAI-managed hosted tool that performs semantic and keyword retrieval over vector-store files and adds `file_citation` annotations. In function calling, the model requests a call, and application code executes the function and returns the result. An application inside the internal network can therefore query inventory directly when asked.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Inventory retrieval is appropriate, but manual retrieval requires operating an embedding pipeline and vector database, violating [no self-operated retrieval infrastructure].
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Added vector-store files are searchable only after their status reaches `completed`. Replacing snapshots every minute still cannot guarantee values current at question time.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Slowly changing large documents use managed retrieval and file citations; rapidly changing values use application-executed functions inside the internal network. All three constraints are satisfied.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: OpenAI describes remote MCP servers as servers on the public internet. Exposing inventory this way violates the prohibition, and data sent to an MCP server follows that server's policies.

Additional note: OpenAI also documents Secure MCP Tunnel for connecting private MCP servers without public exposure. However, if the application already runs inside the internal network, function calling satisfies the requirements without another component.

**References**: [File search](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-file-search) · [Function calling](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling) · [MCP servers](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-connectors-mcp) · [MCP servers › Secure MCP Tunnel](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-connectors-mcp)

questions.title: Match knowledge architectures to requirements
questions.prompt:
Choose the **most appropriate** knowledge delivery method on the right for each requirement on the left. One method is unused.

| Requirement | Knowledge delivery method |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Repeatedly reference dozens of large contract PDFs across many days and requests in the Claude API without resending the originals every time | a. Gemini API File Search store + file metadata filters |
| 2. Handle thousands of PDFs with the Gemini API, narrow retrieval by department, and avoid operating retrieval infrastructure | b. Pass retrieved results in Claude API `search_result` content blocks + enable citations |
| 3. Include public news and prices published today in Gemini API answers | c. Periodically fine-tune the model on document contents |
| 4. Cite internal documents found by a custom search engine in the Claude API, including source and title | d. Upload once through the Claude Files API and reference by `file_id` |
| 5. Store embeddings alongside existing operational PostgreSQL data in the same managed database on Google Cloud | e. Grounding with Google Search |
| | f. Agent Platform + AlloyDB for PostgreSQL RAG reference architecture |

options.text: Gemini API File Search store + file metadata filters
Pass retrieved results in Claude API `search_result` content blocks + enable citations
Periodically fine-tune the model on document contents
Upload once through the Claude Files API and reference by `file_id`
Grounding with Google Search
Agent Platform + AlloyDB for PostgreSQL RAG reference architecture

items.text: Repeatedly reference dozens of large contract PDFs across many days and requests in the Claude API without resending the originals every time

Include public news and prices published today in Gemini API answers

questions.explanation:
| Requirement | Answer | Decisive reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | {{option:d}} | The Files API lets you upload once and reference `file_id` in subsequent Messages requests without resending content. Uploading, retrieving, and deleting files are free; only file content used in requests is billed as input tokens. |
| 2 | {{option:a}} | File Search manages ingestion, chunking, indexing, and retrieval. Files can carry key-value metadata, and `metadata_filter` can restrict retrieval to a document subset. |
| 3 | {{option:e}} | Grounding with Google Search lets the model decide whether to search, run queries, and ground answers in real-time web content. |
| 4 | {{option:b}} | `search_result` blocks let the model cite user-provided results like web search results. They can appear in tool results or top-level user-message content. |
| 5 | {{option:f}} | Google Cloud's AlloyDB for PostgreSQL RAG reference architecture suits storing vector embeddings in the same managed database as operational data. |
| (Unused) | {{option:c}} | OpenAI's accuracy guide distinguishes context optimization for missing, current, or internal knowledge from LLM optimization such as fine-tuning for consistent behavior, format, or tone. All five requirements concern knowledge delivery, so fine-tuning is never the best fit. |

Additional note: Gemini API File Search cannot be combined with Grounding with Google Search in one request. An application needing both requirements 2 and 3 must split requests. Files uploaded to the Claude Files API are workspace-wide rather than user-scoped and are not ZDR-eligible, so multi-customer services and ZDR organizations require separate review.

questions.title: Reducing retrieval failures caused by contextless chunks
questions.prompt:
A RAG system using embedding-only retrieval over tens of thousands of supply contracts, totaling hundreds of millions of tokens, frequently fails to retrieve relevant passages. Analysis finds that chunks such as "revenue for the quarter increased 3% from the previous quarter" lack company names or dates and cannot be connected to questions. The team uses the experiments in Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval article as its expected-effect benchmark. Requirements:

- Reduce top-20-chunk retrieval failure rate by **at least 60% from the current baseline**.
- **A small increase in query latency is acceptable**.
- **Minimize preprocessing costs**, including generating chunk descriptions.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Add document context to each chunk and build Contextual Embeddings and Contextual BM25 indexes. Cache documents during description generation, but omit reranking to avoid increased latency.
Build Contextual Embeddings and Contextual BM25 indexes, rerank the initial top 150 results down to 20, and reuse documents through prompt caching when generating descriptions.

Build Contextual Embeddings and Contextual BM25 indexes and add reranking. To reduce preprocessing time, generate descriptions in parallel by attaching the full document to every chunk without caching.
Apply only Contextual Embeddings without a new BM25 index, and use prompt caching for descriptions at approximately $1.02 per million document tokens.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are [at least 60% reduction] and [minimum preprocessing cost]; [small latency increase acceptable] permits reranking. In the article's experiments, top-20 retrieval failure fell from a 5.7% baseline by 35% with Contextual Embeddings alone (to 3.7%), 49% with Contextual BM25 added (to 2.9%), and 67% when the top 150 results were reranked down to 20 (to 1.9%). Reranking adds some latency and cost. The article also estimates one-time preprocessing at around $1.02 per million document tokens when each document is cached once and reused to generate chunk-specific context.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Preprocessing cost is minimized, but the 49% reduction without reranking misses [at least 60%]. There is no need to omit reranking when a small latency increase is permitted.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: The article's strongest combination achieves a 67% reduction, exceeding the target, while caching minimizes preprocessing cost. The tradeoff is slightly higher query latency, explicitly allowed here.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Retrieval quality matches {{option:B}}, but sending the full document for every chunk without caching bills the same document tokens repeatedly, violating [minimum preprocessing cost].
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: The $1.02 cost figure is correct, but Contextual Embeddings alone reduce failures only 35%, far short of the target.

Additional note: The article recommends testing the number of reranked chunks per use case: more can improve performance but increase latency and cost. It also suggests putting an entire knowledge base under 200,000 tokens into the prompt without RAG, but that does not apply to hundreds of millions of tokens.

**References**: [Introducing Contextual Retrieval › Introducing Contextual Retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval) · [Introducing Contextual Retrieval › Using Prompt Caching to reduce the costs of Contextual Retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval) · [Introducing Contextual Retrieval › Further boosting performance with Reranking](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

questions.title: Designing departmental document retrieval with Gemini API File Search
questions.prompt:
An internal document-search service uses Gemini API File Search. The requirements are:

- Finance, HR, and sales documents are mixed together, but users must **search only their own department's documents**, regardless of user input.
- Original documents total approximately 5 GB, and indexed store size is estimated at three times original size. Some documents change weekly, and **indexing cost must be controlled**.
- Follow documented operational recommendations to meet search-latency targets.

Choose **two** design decisions that meet these requirements.

options.text: Put all documents in one store and handle department separation through system instructions saying to use only the questioner's department, populated by the server.
Attach department metadata to each imported file, use one store of approximately 15 GB after indexing, and have the server insert the user's department into `metadata_filter`.
Import approximately 300 GB of company-wide file-server documents into one store to accommodate future growth, and have the server add a department `metadata_filter`.
Create a new store weekly, reimport all documents, switch queries to it, then delete the old store, which serves traffic during the transition.
Reimport only changed documents each week and retain other indexes because indexing embeddings are billed, while store storage and query-time embeddings are free.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [search only the user's department], [control indexing cost], and [search-latency criteria]. File Search is managed RAG that automatically imports, chunks, embeds, and indexes files. String/numeric metadata can be attached to files, and `metadata_filter` restricts documents at query time. Only indexing embeddings incur embedding charges; storage and query-time embeddings are free, while retrieved-document tokens incur normal context-token charges. Documentation recommends stores under 20 GB for latency.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: All documents remain retrieval candidates, so other departments' documents can enter model context. Instructions merely ask the model and cannot enforce retrieval scope, violating [search only the user's department] independently of input.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Approximately 15 GB meets the under-20-GB recommendation, and server-inserted department filters enforce scope independently of user input.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Filters enforce separation, but a 300-GB store greatly exceeds the under-20-GB recommendation, violating [search-latency criteria]. It may also hit tier-specific total-capacity limits.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It can transition without downtime and retain filters, but re-bills indexing embeddings for every document weekly, violating [control indexing cost].
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: It identifies the billed component, indexing embeddings, and controls cost by reindexing only changes.

Also note: Separate departmental stores provide stronger separation. Either filter or store selection must be server-enforced. Original files uploaded via the File API expire after 48 hours, but imported store data remains until deleted.

questions.title: Choosing a cache TTL for an interactive service with long request intervals
questions.prompt:
An internal legal-advice tool uses Claude Sonnet 5.5 through the Claude API. Every request begins with a fixed prefix of approximately 40,000 tokens containing tool definitions and the full policy text in the system prompt, followed by a user question. Usage and requirements are:

- Requests arrive throughout the day at average intervals of 15–20 minutes.
- The **entire policy must always be referenced**, regardless of question type; clauses cannot be omitted.
- The current five-minute TTL cache almost always reports zero `cache_read_input_tokens`.
- Users need immediate conversational answers, so **latency must not increase**, and **input cost must decrease**.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Keep the five-minute TTL and move the `cache_control` breakpoint to the end of the changing user-question block.
Remove the full policy from the system prompt and retrieve approximately 3,000 tokens of relevant clauses by vector search for each question.
Set `cache_control` with a one-hour TTL (`"ttl": "1h"`) on the final block of the fixed prefix.
Send requests through the Message Batches API for a 50% discount.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [15–20-minute request intervals] and [latency must not increase]. Claude prompt caching caches the prefix in tools → system → messages order through the block containing `cache_control`. A five-minute cache expires between 15–20-minute requests, preventing hits. One-hour writes cost twice the base input rate; Sonnet 5.5 reads cost 0.05 times base, and documentation says a one-hour write passes break-even after two reads. Place the breakpoint on the last block that stays identical across requests.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: A breakpoint on changing content creates new entries without hits. It also leaves TTL expiration unresolved, failing [reduce input cost].
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It reduces input tokens, but adds retrieval to each question, violating [no latency increase], and omits unselected policy clauses from model input, violating [always reference the entire policy].
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: A TTL longer than the request interval preserves the prefix and reduces input cost without added latency.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It provides a 50% discount, but asynchronous batches, mostly within one hour and up to 24 hours, cannot provide immediate conversational responses.

Also note: There are at most four explicit cache breakpoints per request. Sonnet 5.5 requires at least 512 cacheable tokens; shorter inputs are silently uncached. Check `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` for cache behavior.

**References**: [Prompt caching (Claude) › Pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) · [Prompt caching (Claude) › Best practices for effective caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) · [Pricing › Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) · [Batch processing › Batch limitations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing)

questions.title: Processing an overnight bulk classification workload
questions.prompt:
An e-commerce company using the OpenAI Responses API must classify around 30,000 new product descriptions into categories each night. Requirements:

- Results are needed **only before work begins the following morning**.
- **Minimize cost**.
- International customers still generate real-time chat traffic overnight, so classification **must not consume per-model rate limits for synchronous requests**.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Bundle requests into a JSONL file and submit them to the Batch API with a `24h` completion window.
Use synchronous calls with `service_tier` set to `"priority"` to finish classification quickly.
Use standard synchronous calls, placing shared classification instructions at the start of the prompt to receive cache discounts.
Parallelize synchronous overnight calls to finish quickly and retry failures with exponential backoff.

questions.explanation:
The OpenAI Batch API processes requests asynchronously at a 50% discount compared with synchronous APIs, with a 24-hour completion window. Batch rate limits are managed separately from synchronous per-model limits, so batch usage does not consume standard model limits. A batch supports up to 50,000 requests and a 200MB input file, allowing 30,000 requests in one submission.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It satisfies the deadline (next morning), cost, and protection of synchronous limits.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Priority tokens cost more than standard tokens, and documentation advises against using Priority for data processing or evaluations. Priority shares per-model rate limits with standard processing.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Caching lowers input costs for the shared portion, but the remainder is full-price, and synchronous calls consume the same model limits as real-time chat. Note that `24h` is currently the only configurable Batch completion window.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Synchronous calls are billed at full price and share model limits with real-time chat. Failed requests also count toward per-minute limits.

questions.title: Balancing cost and completion in a Flex evaluation pipeline
questions.prompt: Weekly model evaluations and data enrichment jobs run on the OpenAI API with `service_tier: "flex"`. Each request contains the same evaluation instructions and rubric, several thousand tokens long, followed by the sample. Requests occasionally fail because capacity is unavailable, and some responses are very slow. Requirements are **minimum cost normally** and **assured completion near the weekly report deadline**. Select **2** operational designs consistent with the documentation.

options.text: Flex `429 Resource Unavailable` responses are billed, so limit retries to one to save money and defer remaining failures to next week.
Normally retry `429 Resource Unavailable` with exponential backoff. Near the deadline, retry using standard processing by changing `service_tier` to `auto`.
Keep shared evaluation instructions and rubrics at the start and append samples afterward to combine Flex pricing with prompt caching discounts.
Move the entire evaluation pipeline to Priority processing for stable responses.
Immediately retry failed Flex `429` requests with faster-than-standard Priority processing (`service_tier: "priority"`) to eliminate weekly deadline risk.

questions.explanation:
Flex processes Responses and Chat Completions requests at Batch API rates, with additional prompt caching discounts, in exchange for slower responses and occasional capacity shortages. It suits low-priority evaluations, data enrichment, and asynchronous work. Insufficient capacity returns `429 Resource Unavailable`, and these requests are not billed. Documentation offers two strategies: exponential backoff when delay is tolerable, or standard-processing retries when completion is important.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; factual error)**: `429 Resource Unavailable` requests are not billed, so cost is not a reason to limit retries.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It applies the two documented retry strategies to cost-first and completion-first periods.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: OpenAI caching requires exact prefix matches. Fixed content first and changing samples last enables cache discounts with Flex too.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Priority costs more per token than standard, and documentation says not to use it for data processing or evaluation jobs.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; appropriate to another situation)**: The documented completion-oriented alternative is retrying with standard processing. Priority targets latency-sensitive user-facing services, and using it for evaluations conflicts with the guidance.

questions.title: Combining Provisioned Throughput commitments for a short seasonal peak
questions.prompt:
A customer support service uses a Gemini model on the global endpoint of Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Capacity planning shows:

- Normal demand is nearly constant all year and needs **17 GSU**.
- A promotion doubles demand to **34 GSU** for **only two weeks** in mid-December.
- This is a real-time service, so **required throughput must be guaranteed** during both normal and peak periods.
- Finance approves the plan with **the lowest total annual cost**, excluding promotional credits.

**Reference rates for this calculation**

The global Provisioned Throughput rates per GSU-hour are:

| Commitment term | Rate per GSU-hour |
| --- | ---: |
| 1 week | $7.14 |
| 1 month | Approximately $3.70 |
| 3 months | Approximately $3.29 |
| 1 year | Approximately $2.74 |

**Calculation assumptions**: 1 week = 168 hours · 1 month = 730 hours · 1 year = 8,760 hours

**Which configuration guarantees the required throughput at the lowest total annual cost?**

options.text: Buy 34 GSU with a 1-year commitment to guarantee peak capacity all year and fix annual costs without additional purchases or renewals.
Buy 17 GSU with a 1-year commitment and add 17 GSU on a 1-month commitment in December to cover the two-week peak.
Renew 17 GSU on monthly commitments, increase to 34 GSU at the December renewal, then return to 17 GSU in January.
Buy 17 GSU with a 1-year commitment and add 17 GSU through two consecutive 1-week commitments during the two-week peak.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [guaranteed throughput], [minimum annual total cost], and the [two-week peak]. Agent Platform pricing describes Provisioned Throughput as guaranteed throughput, purchased in GSU with 1-week, 1-month, 3-month, or 1-year commitments. All four options guarantee throughput, so cost determines the answer. Although annual commitments have the lowest hourly price, committing long term to short-lived additional demand charges for unused periods. Match the additional commitment duration to the demand period.

| Configuration | Calculation (period cost per GSU × GSU count) | Approximate annual total |
| --- | --- | --- |
| {{option:A}} | $24,000 (annual) × 34 | $816,000 |
| {{option:B}} | $24,000 × 17 + $2,700 (monthly) × 17 | $453,900 |
| {{option:C}} | $2,700 × 17 × 12 + $2,700 × 17 | $596,700 |
| {{option:D}} | $24,000 × 17 + $1,200 (weekly) × 17 × 2 | $448,800 |

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Throughput is guaranteed, but the additional 17 GSU needed for two weeks sit unused for 50 weeks, producing the highest total cost.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: A month for the additional 17 GSU costs about $2,700 per GSU, exceeding the approximately $2,400 for two weekly commitments.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: It adapts flexibly, but buying constant baseline demand monthly costs roughly $8,400 more per GSU annually than an annual commitment.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: The cheapest annual commitment covers steady demand, and weekly commitments match the two-week increase, satisfying guaranteed throughput and minimum total cost. The tradeoff is managing two additional purchases around peak season.

Additional note: For a peak lasting four weeks or more, one month (about $2,700 per GSU) is cheaper than four weeks (about $4,800), favoring {{option:B}}. Documentation also illustrates calculating required GSU using model-specific throughput, such as 57,000 tokens/second → 17 GSU.

questions.title: Preventing an internal analytics tool from consuming production rate limits
questions.prompt:
An organization runs a customer support service and an internal analyst reporting tool with Claude Sonnet 5.5 through the Claude API. Both use API keys from the Default workspace. At month-end, analyst query spikes exhaust organization-wide ITPM, causing 429 errors for customer support too. Requirements:

- Customer support must **retain access to a share of the organization limit**, even during analytics spikes.
- Analysts wait at their screens, so the tool must remain **interactive, responding within minutes**.
- Implement this month **without new contracts or purchases**.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Move analytics requests to Message Batches: its limits are separate from Messages API per-model limits, so analytics will not consume support capacity.
Create a separate analytics workspace and switch keys, but set no limits; use Console to distinguish its usage and monitor month-end spikes.
Negotiate a Custom tier agreement with sales to raise organizational ITPM/OTPM enough to retain headroom during analytics spikes.
Create a separate analytics workspace, switch to its keys, and set workspace ITPM/OTPM caps below organizational limits.

questions.explanation:
The decisive facts are [both services share the default workspace], [retain interactive operation], and [no new agreement]. Claude API workspace RPM/ITPM/OTPM caps can prevent one workspace from consuming all organizational capacity. Limits cannot be set on the default workspace, so analytics must move to a separate workspace. Unused capacity remains available to other workspaces, and organizational limits always apply.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Batch limits are separate, but despite most batches finishing within an hour, processing can take 24 hours and cannot guarantee interactive answers within minutes.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Separation and usage visibility are appropriate, but unconfigured workspace limits equal organizational limits. Analytics can still exhaust capacity at month-end and cause support 429 errors, violating [reserve a share].
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Higher limits may reduce bottlenecks, but Custom tier requires separate account-team negotiation, violating [this month without a new agreement or purchase]. It also preserves the structure allowing analytics to consume support's share.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It isolates and caps analytics while retaining interactive processing and existing contractual conditions.

Also note: Workspace limits are ceilings, not guaranteed minimum allocations. Analytics must move because the default workspace cannot be capped. The response's `anthropic-workspace-id` header identifies the workspace against which usage was counted.

questions.title: Meeting top-performance requirements in a ZDR organization
questions.prompt:
A medical-analytics company using the Claude API has organization-wide ZDR (Zero Data Retention) coverage. A new task requires prolonged, multistep reasoning, and researchers want the highest-performing model. The conditions are:

- Security requires **this task's data to remain entirely within ZDR coverage**.
- Work must **start this week**, so separate Anthropic approval cannot be awaited.
- Achievement of performance targets must be **reported to management using task evaluation-set results**.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Request a Claude Fable 5.1 ZDR exception from Anthropic, then use the organization's defaults and validate performance with the evaluation set after approval.
Create a separate workspace with Standard data retention, call Claude Fable 5.1 only there, and validate performance with the evaluation set.
Use Claude Opus 5.5 with effort raised to `xhigh` or `max`, validating performance with the task evaluation set.
Immediately deploy Claude Opus 5.5 at default effort and assess performance afterward through research-team feedback.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [process only within ZDR], [start this week], and [report evaluation-set results]. Claude Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1, Fable 5, and Mythos 5 are "Covered Models" requiring 30-day retention and cannot use ZDR without separate Anthropic approval. Requests from organizations with incompatible retention settings are rejected. Opus 5.5 is outside this list, and effort is ZDR-eligible, so evaluating high-effort Opus 5.5 while retaining ZDR is the best option within the constraints. The tradeoff is inability to use Fable 5.1-level maximum capability for this task.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Approval could enable Fable 5.1 with ZDR, but uncertain timing violates [start this week]. Before approval, calls are rejected for retention requirements.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Documentation permits workspace-level 30-day retention, allowing this week's start and evaluation reporting, but task data leaves ZDR coverage, violating [process only within ZDR].
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: It preserves ZDR and immediate start while following the model guide's path of raising Opus 5.5 effort and evaluating, providing performance-report evidence.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It preserves ZDR and immediate start, but default-effort production deployment and retrospective feedback violate [report evaluation-set results].

Also note: The Batch API retains results for 29 days and is outside ZDR coverage, so Batch-based savings do not fit this task.

questions.title: Reducing overnight summary costs while meeting EU processing and no-storage requirements
questions.prompt:
A European fintech company is building customer support assistance using the OpenAI API with GPT-6.1 Sol. Its organization has already obtained ZDR approval and completed the Modified Retention agreement amendment. Requirements:

- Support inference must **run in the EU**.
- Customer conversations and supporting PDFs must **never remain at OpenAI as application state or disk records, even temporarily**.
- Daily conversation summaries run overnight. Several hours are acceptable, but **cost should be approximately half standard processing**.

Select **2** designs that meet the requirements.

options.text: Choose Europe when creating a new project for support, and send the project’s requests to `eu.api.openai.com`.
Bundle overnight summaries through the Batch API, which supports GPT-6.1 Sol with EU data residency, for a 50% discount.
Use the Responses API with `service_tier: "flex"` for overnight summaries at Batch rates, retrying `429` responses with exponential backoff.
Run summaries asynchronously in Responses API background mode to avoid long-request timeouts, then poll for completed results.
Upload supporting PDFs through the Files API, reference them by `file_id`, and delete them through the API immediately after the conversation.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [EU processing], [no state or disk records], and [roughly half standard cost]. All five options work technically, but storage differs by endpoint and execution mode. OpenAI data residency is configured by choosing a region at project creation and using a region-prefixed domain. Non-US regions require abuse-monitoring control approval and a Modified Retention amendment, already satisfied here. The endpoint table lists `/v1/responses` as ZDR-eligible with exceptions, but `/v1/batches` and `/v1/files` are ineligible and retain state until deletion. GPT-6.1 Sol supports Standard, Flex, and Batch in EU residency; Flex processes Responses requests at Batch API prices.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It fulfills [EU processing] through the documented project region plus prefixed-domain configuration.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Residency and discount are correct, but `/v1/batches` is not ZDR-eligible and retains request data as state until deletion.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It keeps the ZDR-eligible Responses endpoint while receiving Batch rates. The tradeoffs are slower responses and occasional unbilled `429 Resource Unavailable` errors, tolerable for an overnight job that may take hours.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Even within Responses, background mode is a ZDR exception that writes response data to disk for approximately 10 minutes to enable polling. It does not lower prices either.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: `/v1/files` is not ZDR-eligible. Immediate deletion still leaves stored state before deletion. Documentation supports including files directly as base64 in requests with data residency.

Additional note: Residency-eligible models released after March 5, 2026 incur a 10% surcharge on data residency endpoints; include it in cost calculations. With ZDR, `store` is always treated as `false`, regardless of the requested value.

questions.title: Configuring ZDR for an Agent Platform service requiring web grounding
questions.prompt: A securities firm governed by the Google Cloud Platform Terms of Service is building market-news summaries on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Answers must be grounded in current web information. Security requires **zero retention of customer data**, specifically **no caches or query logs of any kind**. Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Use Web Grounding for Enterprise, request an abuse-monitoring exception, set `disableCache` to `true`, and leave request-response logging disabled.
Use Grounding with Google Search, request an abuse-monitoring exception, set `disableCache` to `true`, and leave request-response logging disabled.

- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Abuse monitoring, caching, and logging match {{option:A}}, but Google Search grounding's three-day query retention cannot be disabled, violating [no query logs].
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Grounding with Google Maps retains prompts, context, and outputs for 30 days without opt-out. It also does not match the current-web-information requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Grounding is appropriate, but `EPHEMERAL` disables only disk caching. Memory caching, deleted within 24 hours of creation, remains and violates [no caches of any kind].

- (2) Build an evaluation set representative of production traffic and measure the current model’s baseline score.
- (3) Export usage from the Console Usage page to identify deprecated-model usage by API key and model.

items.text: Gradually shift traffic over hours or days using feature flags, and continue running evaluations after the change.

Export usage from the Console Usage page to identify deprecated-model usage by API key and model.

| 4 | (1) Gradual migration + continuous evaluation | Move production traffic only after the comparison passes, then keep monitoring regressions. | OpenAI evaluation guide › Continuous evaluation; OpenAI Priority processing › Traffic migration over hours using feature flags |

questions.title: Planning migrations when several model retirement dates overlap

Automate `shutdown_date` checks, migrate the earliest-retiring `o4-mini` after regression evaluation in the OpenAI Evals dashboard, then move the summary model and `preview` quotation model to production models.

questions.title: Prompt-length pricing tiers in a high-volume classification service
questions.prompt:
An insurer runs claims classification with Claude Haiku 5.5 through the Claude API. It attaches all supporting documents to every claim, producing an average prompt of about 90,000 tokens; the longest 10% exceed 130,000 tokens. Only the system prompt and classification rules, about 4,000 tokens, are shared across requests. Everything else varies by claim. This month's bill greatly exceeds total tokens multiplied by the base rate, and tokens in long requests are billed at higher rates. The architect wants to change the configuration under these conditions:

- Internal evaluations show that **Haiku 5.5 is accurate enough**. Classification information is concentrated at the beginning—the claim form and diagnostic summary—while remaining attachments are for reference.
- Representatives wait at their screens, so **latency targets are strict**.
- **Minimize monthly cost**.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Move all requests to Claude Sonnet 5.5 to eliminate request-length pricing tiers and provide additional accuracy headroom.
Send only requests exceeding 130,000 tokens to the Message Batches API for batch discounts.
Apply prompt caching to the shared system prompt and classification rules so they are billed at cache-read rates.
Keep only the initial documents needed for classification and omit reference attachments so every prompt stays below 100,000 tokens.

questions.explanation:
The decisive cues are [Haiku 5.5 accuracy is sufficient], [higher rates for long requests], and [strict latency]. When a Claude Haiku 5.5 prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens, both input and output rates for that request enter a higher tier—about five times the base tier in the price table. Length is assessed per request, including cache-read and cache-write tokens. Reducing input so requests stay below the 100,000-token tier is therefore the most direct way to lower unit prices.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; overengineering)**: Sonnet 5.5 lacks Haiku 5.5's 100,000-token pricing tier, but its base rates are higher and accuracy is already sufficient. An unnecessary model upgrade conflicts with minimum cost.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Batches discounts input/output by 50%, but processing is asynchronous and results are not immediate, violating strict latency while representatives wait.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; related-feature confusion)**: Cache reads are cheaper but still count toward prompt length. Only about 4,000 tokens are shared, limiting savings; 130,000-token requests remain in the expensive tier.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Since classification information is concentrated at the beginning, omitting reference attachments is likely to preserve accuracy while moving requests below the pricing threshold. Fewer input tokens also help latency. The tradeoff is defining extraction rules and reevaluating accuracy.

Additional note: Requests just below the threshold, such as 99,000 tokens, are classified solely by prompt length regardless of output size. Check the length distribution so extracted inputs do not cluster dangerously close to the threshold.

**References**: [Pricing › Long context pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) · [Context windows](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows) · [Choosing the right model](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/choosing-a-model)

questions.title: Gemini model and invocation method for a 600,000-token input and 150,000-token report
questions.prompt:
Finance is automating quarterly closing reports with the Gemini API. Inputs contain about 600,000 tokens of quarterly financial material; the output is one approximately 150,000-token report with extensive cross-references. Conditions:

- Generate the report **consistently in one pass**. Multiple section-level calls produce mismatched numerical references and are unusable.
- It runs overnight for morning review, so **latency is acceptable**.
- Production policy allows **Stable models only**.
- Include the **entire requested length, about 150,000 tokens**.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Use Gemini 3.8 Flash to create an outline, then call it separately for each section, passing summaries and key figures from earlier sections to later calls.
Call Gemini 4 Argon synchronously with an output cap of 65,536 tokens or less, producing one compressed report focused on essentials.
Call Gemini 4 Argon through Interactions API background execution (long decode), with an output cap comfortably above 150,000 and a low thinking_level.
Use the same Gemini 4 Argon background execution (long decode), but set the output cap to exactly 150,000 and keep default thinking_level.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [consistent one-pass generation] and [150,000 output tokens]. Gemini 3 and 2.5 families have separate 1M input and 64K output budgets, so a single output cannot exceed 64K. Gemini 4 Argon shares one 1M window across input, thinking, and output. Synchronous output is capped at 65,536 tokens; larger output requires Interactions API background execution (long decode). A 600,000-token input plus 150,000-token output fits the window. Since `max_output_tokens` also includes thinking, allow headroom or lower `thinking_level` to preserve the required body length.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Flash's 65,536-token output cap requires splitting sections, violating one-pass consistency.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Compressing within Argon's synchronous cap uses one call but fails the 150,000-token length requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Stable Argon's long decode preserves one call and reduces the risk of thinking consuming the output allowance needed for the report. Tradeoffs are higher-tier model pricing, charges for tokens across every hop (64K generation segment), and long runtime, acceptable overnight.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: The method is right, but setting the cap equal to the target length with default thinking leaves the report short by the thinking tokens consumed. Reaching the cap may also produce `incomplete`.

Additional note: Argon's rates rise on December 1, 2026; estimate costs using the subsequent rates. Documentation says long decode is unsuitable for short interactive requests or prompts near the input limit.

**References**: [Long context](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/long-context) · [Long decode](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/long-decode) · [Gemini thinking › max\_output\_tokens](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thinking) · [Gemini 3.8 Flash](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/models/gemini-3.8-flash) · [Gemini 4 Argon](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/models/gemini-4-argon)

questions.prompt:
Legal is designing a long-contract summarization service with Claude Opus 5.5. It has a 1-million-token context window and supports up to 128,000 output tokens per request. Input, including appendices, can reach 950,000 tokens. Conditions:

- A summary interrupted mid-generation is **unusable**.
- The output allowance must remain **up to 128,000 tokens**.
- **Every clause, including appendices, must be reflected**. Internal evaluation confirms that summarizing groups of clauses separately and combining them preserves quality.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: For inputs above approximately 870,000 tokens, divide them into clause groups, summarize each, and combine them, retaining the 128,000-token output cap.
Send all 950,000 input tokens with a 128,000-token output cap and retry identical requests when responses end because the window is exceeded.
Send all 950,000 input tokens but reduce the output cap to 50,000 so the combined budget fits the window.
Cut appendices from the end to keep input at or below 870,000 tokens while retaining the 128,000-token output cap.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [no interruption] and [allow 128,000 output tokens]. Claude documentation says Opus 5.5 supports a 1M context window and 128k output per request, with thinking always enabled. Input alone exceeding the window causes 400, but a request whose input plus `max_tokens` exceeds the window is accepted and stops when generation reaches the window, with `stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded"`. Subtracting 128,000 from 1 million leaves approximately 870,000 safe input tokens.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Splitting input into groups at or below 870,000 leaves room for the full 128,000 output tokens and processes every clause. Tradeoffs are splitting/merging logic and possible loss of some inter-clause context.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: The request is accepted, but 950,000 plus 128,000 exceeds the window. A long summary stops at the same point again; identical retries do not resolve interruption.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: The combined budget fits, avoiding window interruption, but a 50,000 output cap violates the required 128,000 allowance.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: The budget fits, but omitted appendix clauses violate complete coverage.

**References**: [Context windows › Context window size, Input + max\_tokens vs. the window](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows)

questions.title: Token planning for multi-turn support with thinking enabled
questions.prompt: A customer support app uses Claude Sonnet 5.5 with thinking enabled, with some paths planned on the Gemini API, also with thinking enabled. Sessions exceed 10 turns. **Responses must not be truncated**, and monthly cost and throughput must both be planned. Select **2** token-planning statements consistent with the documentation.

options.text: Because thinking is billed at output rates, estimate monthly costs from output including thinking, not visible answer length alone.
To cap Claude costs, set `max_tokens` close to visible answer length and do not account for thinking separately.
For Claude models retaining prior thinking blocks by default, include their accumulation as input in context usage and input-cost estimates.
Plan Claude output-tokens-per-minute limits using average answer length; absorb peak thinking-related 429s through retries.
To reduce Gemini cost without truncating responses, keep default `thinking_level` and only lower `max_output_tokens`.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [no truncated responses] and [monthly cost and throughput planning]. Claude thinking tokens consume part of `max_tokens`, are billed as output, and count toward rate limits. Recent models including Sonnet 5.5 retain earlier thinking blocks by default and count them as input. Gemini also bills thinking with output, and `max_output_tokens` is a hard cutoff including thinking.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Monthly cost estimates must include thinking because it is billed at output rates.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Thinking shares `max_tokens`; a cap based only on answer length may be consumed by thinking and truncate the answer.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Thinking blocks accumulate as input across turns, increasing context usage and input costs. Thinking-block clearing can be used if needed.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Thinking counts toward output limits, so average visible-answer planning easily exceeds limits at peaks. Retrying 429s compensates after the fact for missing capacity planning rather than providing a throughput plan.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Hitting the limit during thinking can leave `incomplete` output with empty or truncated text, while thinking remains billable. Documentation recommends lowering `thinking_level` to reduce cost and latency.

**References**: [Context windows › Thinking blocks from previous turns](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows) · [Gemini thinking › Pricing, max\_output\_tokens](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thinking)

- Preserve the migration's **cost-reduction goal**.

What is the most appropriate action to isolate and address the cause?

options.text: Downgrade again to Claude Haiku 5.5 to cut cost and latency, checking accuracy through production monitoring.
Explicitly set Sonnet 5.5 to medium effort, Opus 5.5’s prior default, and compare accuracy, latency, and output tokens on the same evaluation set.
Lower `max_tokens` to cap output growth, then inspect logs for truncated responses.
Add prompt caching to reduce repeated-prefix processing cost and time, comparing latency against logs from the same period.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [effort never specified] and [maintain accuracy]. Anthropic's defaults differ by model: Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 use `medium`; Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1 use `high`. Effort trades capability against latency/cost within a model. Changing only the model can therefore raise default effort and increase latency/output. First control that variable and compare with the same evaluation set.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: An unevaluated Haiku downgrade gambles with accuracy and does not isolate the cause.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Explicit effort aligns conditions and reuses the evaluation set, meeting minimal-code-change and accuracy requirements. Determine savings from medium-versus-high evaluation results.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: A lower output cap can truncate answers while leaving the underlying cause unchanged, risking accuracy.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; appropriate to another situation)**: Caching reduces repeated input-prefix cost/latency, not the cause of increased output tokens and reasoning time.

**References**: [Choosing the right model › Default effort, Choose the best model to start with](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/choosing-a-model) · [Pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing)

Production allows **Stable models only**, and **cost must be minimized among configurations meeting accuracy**. Which choice is most appropriate?

options.text: Use gemini-3.8-flash, checking thinking level and cost on the same evaluation set before production.
Keep gemini-3.5-flash-lite and improve accuracy using production data after launch.
Use gemini-3.1-pro-preview after validating quality with the same evaluation set.
Use gemini-2.5-flash, checking thinking level and cost with the same evaluation set before production.

The decisive constraints are [new project without usage history] and [Stable only]. Gemini deprecation documentation says 2.5 models have not retired but are restricted to prior users, and recommends 3.5 Flash-Lite or 3.8 Flash for new projects. Since Flash-Lite fails evaluation, 3.8 Flash remains the recommended option and is listed as Stable.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It is recommended for new projects, Stable, and passes accuracy targets.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Launching a model that failed evaluation violates the accuracy requirement.

questions.title: Improving response speed in an interactive code-review assistant
questions.prompt:
An internal code-review assistant uses Claude Opus 5.5. It has an interactive path where developers wait for results and a nightly Batch path reviewing the entire repository. Conditions for improving speed:

- Internal evaluation shows **lower effort or Haiku 5.5 fails accuracy requirements**.
- Changes often span several files, so **cross-file context must remain visible together**.
- **Approximately double monthly cost is acceptable only for the interactive path**.
- **Minimize code changes**.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Lower effort one step on both paths so the same model responds faster.
Switch only the interactive path to Claude Haiku 5.5, keeping nightly Batch on Opus 5.5.
Set `speed: "fast"` only on interactive requests, leaving nightly Batch at standard speed.
Split changed files into separate parallel review calls and combine results to reduce total wait time.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are [lower effort/Haiku fail accuracy] and [double cost permitted only interactively]. Fast mode uses identical model weights to increase output speed by up to 2.5 times on supported Opus models, including Opus 5.5. Enable it with `speed: "fast"`; Opus 5.5 rates are twice standard, $8/$40 per MTok. Intelligence and behavior remain unchanged, and it cannot be combined with Batch API.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Lower effort improves speed but has already failed internal accuracy evaluation.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Haiku 5.5 likewise fails the required accuracy.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Keeping model and effort preserves accuracy, and adding one speed parameter minimizes code changes. The cost is roughly doubled interactive spending. Acceleration affects output tokens per second (OTPS), not time to first token (TTFT); alternating fast and standard speed invalidates cache.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Wait time may fall, but cross-file context is broken. Duplicating shared information across calls also increases input costs.

Additional note: Fast mode has separate rate limits and returns 429 when exceeded. Decide in advance whether to fall back to standard speed.

**References**: [Fast mode](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode) · [Pricing › Fast mode](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) · [Choosing the right model](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/choosing-a-model)

questions.title: Which starting model/effort configurations best fit the three features?
questions.prompt: Choose starting configurations for the production setup using the guide's workflow recommendations. Options list purchase-request classification / consolidated-report draft / executive announcement, in that order.
questions.context:
> **[Company overview]** Hansol Trading is a fictional distributor. Procurement is developing three purchasing assistants with the OpenAI Responses API.
>
> **[Features]**
>
> - **Purchase-request classification**: Classify internal requests by type. Thousands arrive per minute, results immediately feed another system, and nobody waits. Categories are clearly scoped.
> - **Consolidated supplier-change report draft**: Once weekly, combine change requests from several suppliers into a draft that a person revises and finalizes.
> - **Executive announcement editing**: Refine public announcements while preserving facts and tone. Volume is low and quality standards are high.
>
> **[Pilot]** To prioritize quality, all three used Sol · Medium in month one, exceeding the monthly cost target. Each feature already has an evaluation set with known answers and at least 20 questions.
>
> **[Constraints]** Quality criteria differ by feature and total cost must be managed. Evaluation staff can compare settings for only one feature this week.

options.text: Luna · Low / Luna · Low / Luna · Low
Luna · Low / Sol · Medium / Astra · Low
Sol · Medium / Sol · Medium / Sol · Medium
Luna · Low / Astra · Medium / Astra · Low

questions.explanation:
The decisive evidence is the three feature descriptions, pilot cost overrun, and different quality criteria. OpenAI maps simple extraction/clearly scoped problems to Luna · Low, complex work expecting revision and coordinated deliverables to Sol · Medium, and concise writing preserving facts/nuance to Astra · Low. Frequent automation accumulates cost faster.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Cheapest, but Luna · Low does not match consolidated-draft and public-announcement quality needs.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Use the lightest configuration for thousands of classifications per minute, Sol · Medium for weekly drafts expecting revision, and Astra · Low for public wording. All are starting points to refine through comparisons on the same evaluation sets.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Retaining the pilot keeps classification unnecessarily heavy, leaving the monthly cost overrun unresolved.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; overengineering)**: Raising weekly, human-revised drafts to Astra · Medium adds unnecessary capability/effort and total cost.

**References**: [Model selection › Find the right model for your workflow](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-selection) · [Model selection › How to think about models and reasoning effort](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-selection)

Compare purchase classification on Sol · Medium versus Luna · Low using the same set, retaining the lightest passing setting.
