questions.title: Chunking settings for policy clauses split at chunk boundaries
questions.prompt:
An internal Q&A assistant uses managed file search—OpenAI file_search or Gemini File Search—over a roughly 400-page policy manual. Clauses are numbered, with lengthy exception conditions; the longest clause is about 900 tokens. Validation finds a clause split at a chunk boundary, causing citation of its main text without exceptions. Conditions:

- Only **one developer** is available; a separate document parser cannot be built.
- Policies change **monthly** and can be reingested then.
- **Clause citations omitting exceptions are prohibited**.
- Thousands of daily queries require managing **per-request cost and latency**.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Increase maximum chunk size and overlap so the longest clause fits intact in at least one chunk, then reingest and remeasure using the same questions.
Build a custom preprocessing script splitting the manual by clause number into separate files, rerunning it each revision.
Increase the number of retrieved results so the following chunk is also sent, letting the model join fragments.
Eliminate retrieval and send the full policy manual with every prompt to avoid chunk boundaries.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [one developer] and [no citations missing exceptions]. Managed retrieval allows ingestion-time chunk size and overlap settings. OpenAI vector stores use static `max_chunk_size_tokens` and `chunk_overlap_tokens`; Gemini File Search uses `chunking_config` with `max_tokens_per_chunk` and `max_overlap_tokens`. Documentation examples are approximately 1,200/200 and 200/20 respectively. If overlap is at least as long as the longest clause, every clause appears intact in some chunk.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Configuration changes and monthly reingestion avoid custom development. Reusing evaluation questions verifies improvement. Tradeoffs are larger per-query input from larger chunks and larger indexes from overlap.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Clause-based splitting may work, but creating and maintaining preprocessing code conflicts with the staffing constraint.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: More results do not guarantee retrieval of the exception chunk, and asking the model to join fragments makes complete citation requirements difficult to satisfy.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; overengineering)**: Boundaries disappear, but sending 400 pages on every query greatly increases cost and latency.

Additional note: Defaults and allowed ranges differ by product; check documentation before configuring. Adding context descriptions to chunk prefixes is a separate technique.

**References**: [Retrieval (OpenAI) › Static chunking](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/retrieval) · [File Search (Gemini API) › Chunking configuration](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/file-search)

questions.title: Formatting custom search results for citations and no-result handling in Claude
questions.prompt:
An internal assistant retrieves documents with a custom search engine and returns them as Claude API tool results to produce answers with source titles. Requirements:

- Every answer includes **citable source titles**.
- Requests containing tool results are **accepted without validation errors**.
- With zero results, **the conversation continues** and Claude explains the situation.

Which implementation is most appropriate?

options.text: Concatenate results as ordinary text with titles/URLs, returning a plain text block saying no results when empty.
Enable citations only for internal-wiki results, disable them for external documents, and include all as `search_result` blocks in one tool result.
Use `search_result` blocks with citations enabled for all results, but mark the tool result as an error when none are found.
Use `search_result` blocks with uniformly enabled citations; return a plain text block when no results are found.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are citable source titles and continued conversation with no results. Claude `search_result` blocks contain `source`, `title`, and `content`. Citations default off and require `citations: {enabled: true}`. All results in a request must have citations either uniformly enabled or uniformly disabled; mixing causes errors. Inside tool results, `search_result` cannot mix with other block types. With no results, documentation recommends plain text rather than an error.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: It works and handles empty results correctly, but ordinary text does not enable `search_result` citation functionality.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Inconsistent citation settings cause request validation failure.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; appropriate to another situation)**: An empty search should return plain guidance, not an error. Error status is for actual tool failure.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It follows formatting, citation consistency, and no-results rules. Put supplementary explanation inside `search_result.content`, not a separate text block.

Additional note: `search_result` is a standard feature requiring no beta header and supports text only. If web search is used in the same request, enable citations on every `search_result`.

**References**: [Search results › Search result rules, Citation consistency, No results](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/search-results)

questions.title: Revoked documents remaining searchable briefly after deletion
questions.prompt:
An HR-policy assistant uses OpenAI file_search. Whenever access to a disciplinary-case file is revoked, the document is deleted from the vector store. Audit notes that its contents may remain in search results briefly after deletion. Conditions:

- Revocation must take effect **immediately**.
- A small development team needs **low operational burden**.
- Tens of thousands of documents make **full reindexing costs unacceptable**.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Collect revocations and delete them nightly, allowing sufficient time for deletion to propagate before continuing service.
For every revocation, create a new vector store, reingest all remaining documents, then delete the old store.
Give each document a doc_id attribute, add revoked IDs to an application blocklist, enforce exclusion filters on every search, then delete the files.
Add a system instruction not to use documents scheduled for deletion, and continue normal deletion.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are immediate revocation and avoiding full reindexing. OpenAI states vector-store file deletion is eventually consistent, so removed files may briefly remain searchable. Files support up to 16 attributes, and file_search `filters` supports comparison operators including `eq`, `ne`, `in`, and `nin`. Server-enforced exclusion at search time blocks access immediately regardless of deletion propagation.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Documents remain searchable until the batch deletion and propagation delay finish. Eventual consistency cannot guarantee immediate effect.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; overengineering)**: It excludes documents but reindexes tens of thousands per revocation, imposing high cost and operations.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Retrieval-stage filtering immediately blocks access with a simple application blocklist and one attribute. Remove IDs from the list after deletion fully propagates. Tradeoffs are enforcing filters on every call and managing doc_id during ingestion.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Instructions influence model behavior but do not prevent retrieval. Delegating access control to model instructions fails the audit requirement.

**References**: [Retrieval (OpenAI) › Attribute filtering, Vector store file deletion](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/retrieval) · [File search (OpenAI)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-file-search)

questions.title: Exact part-number documents ranked below semantically similar results
questions.prompt: An OpenAI file_search maintenance assistant retrieves semantically similar parts before the document containing an exact part number such as `KX-4471-B`. You want to raise exact-term matches while retaining semantic retrieval benefits. Which setting change is most appropriate?

options.text: Increase `hybrid_search.text_weight` to emphasize keyword matches while retaining `embedding_weight`.
Raise `max_num_results` to its maximum of 50, hoping the correct document reaches the model.
Raise `score_threshold` to remove low-scoring results and emphasize exact part-number documents.
Enable `rewrite_query` to rewrite the user’s input into a search-friendly query.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are exact part-number matching and retained semantic benefits. OpenAI file_search combines embedding and keyword results through reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). In `ranking_options.hybrid_search`, `embedding_weight` and `text_weight` control their relative influence. Higher text weight strengthens exact text matches; at least one weight must exceed zero.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It balances stronger exact matching with retained semantic retrieval.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: More results may include the answer but do not change ranking and add noise/token costs.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: A higher threshold removes low scores; if the exact document scores poorly, it may disappear entirely.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; related-feature confusion)**: Query rewriting turns conversational follow-ups into standalone searches. It does not address ranking for an already complete part-number query.

**References**: [Retrieval (OpenAI) › Ranking, hybrid search weights](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/retrieval)

questions.title: Initial ingestion of 20,000 PDFs into a vector store
questions.prompt: Plan an initial upload of 20,000 PDFs to an OpenAI vector store. Later searches must **narrow to a specific filename** or **filter by department/year**. Avoid **retry backlogs caused by per-minute ingestion limits**. Select **2** correct decisions.

options.text: Submit additions through `file_batches`, with no more than 500 files per request.
Send individual additions in parallel as fast as possible and queue 429 failures for sequential retry.
Put the filename as text on each PDF’s first page and include it in queries to narrow documents semantically.
Explicitly assign a `filename` attribute during ingestion when filename filtering is required, alongside department/year attributes.
Use separate vector stores by department/year and decide not to support filename narrowing.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are avoiding per-minute limit backlogs and filename filtering. OpenAI Retrieval states that `files` and `file_batches` additions share a combined 300-request-per-minute limit. A file batch supports up to 500 files and is recommended for high-throughput ingestion. A `filename` filter matches only an explicitly assigned `filename` attribute.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Batching 20,000 files in groups of 500 takes about 40 requests, comfortably below the limit.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Individual additions share the same 300/minute cap, so flooding 20,000 calls creates 429s and retry queues.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Semantic search considers filenames probabilistically; it is not an exact narrowing filter.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Assign filename attributes at ingestion, then combine them with department/year in filters.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Department/year separation works, but separate stores do not provide filename filtering and abandon a requirement.

**References**: [Retrieval (OpenAI) › Attributes, Attribute filtering, Rate limits](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/retrieval)

questions.title: Launching a 12GB indexed store next week from a Tier 1 project
questions.prompt:
An internal Gemini API File Search service must launch next week. Source documents total 4GB, becoming approximately 12GB after indexing at three times source size. The project is Tier 1; its first payment was 14 days ago, and cumulative spending is about $40. Conditions:

- Launch is in **seven days**.
- **All documents are required**; a partial launch is prohibited.
- Necessary **additional spending can be authorized this week**.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Split into two 6GB stores to stay within each store’s limit, and search both.
Bring cumulative spending to $100 to meet Tier 2 requirements, then ingest everything into one store.
Omit older documents to keep indexed size below 10GB, adding the rest later.
Bring cumulative spending to $1,000 for Tier 3 and ingest everything into one store.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are a seven-day launch and complete coverage. Gemini File Search limits total project store size to Free 1GB, Tier 1 10GB, Tier 2 100GB, and Tier 3 1TB. Size includes inputs and stored embeddings, approximately three times source size. Tier 2 requires $100 in cumulative payments and three days since first payment; Tier 3 requires $1,000 and 30 days. Tiers automatically increase when conditions are met.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Limits apply to the combined project stores, not each store; 12GB still exceeds 10GB.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: The three-day condition is already met; only spending remains, achievable within a week. Tradeoffs are additional spending and possible rejection during upgrade review. Tier 2's 100GB accommodates all documents in one store.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Size fits, but complete-document coverage is violated.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Only 14 days have elapsed; Tier 3's 30-day requirement cannot be reached before launch. Spending alone cannot solve it.

**References**: [File Search (Gemini API) › Limits](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/file-search) · [Rate limits (Gemini API) › Usage tiers](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits)

questions.title: Configuring File Search to retrieve diagram images
questions.prompt:
A Gemini API File Search product-manual service currently uses text-only embeddings. It now needs to retrieve diagram PNGs as images. Some teams also want training videos in the same store. Conditions:

- **The diagram image itself must be searchable**, not merely a textual description.
- A tight schedule and **limited staff** rule out a separate video transcription pipeline this release.
- Search results must allow **downloading the original image**.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Convert diagrams to OCR descriptions and ingest them alongside documents in the existing text-only store.
Create transcripts from video audio and ingest them with documents into a new store.
Add PNG files directly to the existing text-only store and expect them to be searchable with documents.
Reingest documents and PNGs into a new store specifying `gemini-embedding-2`, excluding video from this release.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are image retrieval itself and limited staffing. Gemini File Search uses `gemini-embedding-001` for text embeddings; image retrieval requires specifying `gemini-embedding-2` when creating the store. PNG/JPEG images up to 4K × 4K are supported. Citations include `media_id`, enabling original downloads through `downloadMedia`. Audio/video formats are unsupported.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: It works but retrieves text descriptions, not images, and cannot provide original-image downloads.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Transcripts indirectly support videos but require a new pipeline, conflicting with staffing limits.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; related-feature confusion)**: Documentation requires `gemini-embedding-2` at store creation for image retrieval; there is no basis for expecting text-only configuration to satisfy it.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: A new image-embedding store meets image needs; video is excluded as unsupported. Tradeoffs are reingestion and deferring video requirements.

Additional note: Consider separate video solutions such as transcription later. File-size and tier-based store limits also apply to multimodal stores.

**References**: [File Search (Gemini API) › Multimodal support](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/file-search)

questions.title: Estimating monthly costs for a Gemini File Search FAQ bot
questions.prompt: A team plans an internal FAQ bot using Gemini File Search. Documents total 2GB and are fully reingested monthly. Retrieved chunks become model input for every query. Which monthly cost-estimation method is most appropriate?

options.text: Multiply store capacity by a monthly storage rate, then add reingestion and query input costs.
Charge query embeddings for every query plus retrieved-chunk input tokens, estimating proportionally to query volume.
Add monthly reindexing embedding costs and per-query retrieved-chunk input costs, with zero storage and query-embedding charges.
Calculate embedding costs from indexed size, about three times source size, then add storage charges.

questions.explanation:
The decisive facts are monthly full reingestion and retrieved chunks included in each query's input. Gemini File Search charges embedding rates when files are indexed, while store storage and query-time embeddings are free. Retrieved document tokens are billed as ordinary context tokens. Monthly reindexing embeddings and query input tokens are therefore the two cost components.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; factual error)**: Storage is free.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; factual error)**: Query-time embeddings are free; charging them per query overestimates cost.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: This matches the documented cost structure. Reingestion frequency and chunks per query determine spending.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; related-feature confusion)**: Three-times-source indexed size is used for capacity limits, not billing; storage is also free.

Additional note: Prices change, so remember the structure and verify rates on the pricing page. Smaller chunks or fewer retrieval results reduce per-query input tokens.

**References**: [File Search (Gemini API) › Pricing](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/file-search) · [Gemini API pricing](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing)

questions.title: Insurance RAG balancing EU regulation, large-scale search, and a small team
questions.prompt:
A European insurer is building claims-document RAG on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, formerly Vertex AI. Requirements:

- Guarantee **EU processing and storage** of documents and embeddings.
- **Low-latency retrieval** over tens of millions of chunks.
- Only **two operations staff**.
- Departmental **access separation and auditing**.
- Embedding indexes must have **permissions and lifecycle separate from the operational claims database**.

Which candidate is most appropriate?

options.text: Use Agent Platform RAG Engine in an EU region with VPC Service Controls and customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).
Use Agent Platform Vector Search in an EU region, building ingestion, chunking, embedding, departmental access separation, and auditing yourself.
Build and operate a custom open-source RAG stack on GKE and Cloud SQL in an EU region.
Store embeddings alongside operational claims data in the same AlloyDB for PostgreSQL database in an EU region.

questions.explanation:
The decisive tradeoff is EU processing/storage, low-latency tens-of-millions-scale retrieval, and only two operations staff. RAG Engine supports VPC-SC/CMEK but explicitly lacks data residency. RAG reference architectures describe Vector Search as fully managed serverless high-performance retrieval at scale; GKE/Cloud SQL offers maximum control with the greatest operational burden. AlloyDB places embeddings beside operational data. Location documentation lists several EU Vector Search regions and the general rule that data stays stored/processed in the chosen region, excluding experimental/preview features.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Managed convenience and access controls fit, but unsupported residency violates EU regulation.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: EU-hosted serverless large-scale search meets residency and scale. The tradeoff is building ingestion/chunking/embedding pipelines plus access separation and audits, a substantial burden for two staff that also needs implementation time.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Residency can be met, but self-operating every component is too burdensome for two staff.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Managed database operations are lighter, but colocating embeddings with claims data fails separate permissions/lifecycle. Documentation also provides weaker support for tens-of-millions-scale low-latency retrieval.

Additional note: Regional availability and residency scope can change. Recheck target-region availability and GA status before design.

**References**: [RAG Engine overview › Security and compliance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/build/rag-engine/rag-overview) · [RAG reference architectures](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/rag-reference-architectures) · [Agent Platform locations › Data residency](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/general/locations)

questions.title: Reference architectures for relationship queries and direct open-source control
questions.prompt:
Design two different internal RAG services on Google Cloud. Select **2** reference architectures, one best matching each service.

- Service 1, supplier-risk analysis: Suppliers, parts, and contracts form multistep relationships. **Relationship-traversing queries** such as finding contracts containing a supplier's parts that meet conditions are central.
- Service 2, research portal: The platform team must assemble containerized open-source tools such as Ray and LangChain for **fine-grained component control**, accepting the operational burden.
- Both already have build/deployment pipelines.

options.text: Agent Platform with Vector Search for fully managed serverless large-scale vector retrieval
Agent Platform with Spanner Graph for GraphRAG combining vector search and knowledge-graph queries
Agent Platform with AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, storing embeddings beside operational data
Open-source components on GKE and Cloud SQL for full control of the retrieval layer
A Harness CI/CD pipeline automating RAG application build and deployment

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are Service 1's relationship traversal and Service 2's detailed component control. Google Cloud describes GraphRAG as combining vector retrieval with knowledge-graph queries over interconnected data. GKE/Cloud SQL offers maximum control when building custom applications with open-source tools. The documentation explains tradeoffs rather than a separate selection matrix; this question maps each architecture's intended needs to the scenario.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; appropriate to another situation)**: It targets large workloads with managed serverless operation, not relationship traversal or detailed component control.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It fits Service 1's interconnected-data queries, at the cost of additional graph modeling.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; appropriate to another situation)**: It fits colocating embeddings with operational data in a managed database, which is not required here.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It fits Service 2's direct assembly of Ray/LangChain and other open-source components, with greater operational burden.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; related-feature confusion)**: It addresses continuous integration/deployment, not retrieval-store architecture; both services already have deployment pipelines.

**References**: [RAG reference architecture catalog](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/rag-reference-architectures)

questions.title: Assessing knowledge-architecture statements
questions.prompt:
An architect explains the following to a team designing an internal knowledge assistant. Mark each statement Yes if consistent with provider documentation, otherwise No.

1. Inconsistent response format or tone should be addressed through optimization for consistent model behavior rather than supplying more knowledge with RAG.
2. Incorrect RAG answers may result from retrieving the wrong context or misusing correctly retrieved context; the remedies differ.
3. Long-context models have replaced RAG, summarization, and similar techniques, so documentation generally recommends inserting complete documents.
4. Google Search grounding includes information beyond the model's knowledge cutoff with source citations.

items.text: Inconsistent response format or tone should be addressed through optimization for consistent model behavior rather than supplying more knowledge with RAG.
Incorrect RAG answers may result from retrieving the wrong context or misusing correctly retrieved context; the remedies differ.
Long-context models have replaced RAG, summarization, and similar techniques, so documentation generally recommends inserting complete documents.
Google Search grounding includes information beyond the model's knowledge cutoff with source citations.

questions.explanation:
- **1 (Yes)**: OpenAI distinguishes context problems, meaning missing knowledge, from behavioral consistency problems. Format inconsistency and tone errors belong to model optimization rather than context optimization/RAG.
- **2 (Yes)**: The same guide distinguishes retrieval failures—wrong or excessive irrelevant context—from model failures, where correct context is misused. Improve retrieval quality for the former and instructions for the latter.
- **3 (No)**: Gemini's long-context guide says RAG, summarization, and dropping old messages remain useful in particular scenarios. The ability to provide information upfront does not mean older techniques are obsolete.
- **4 (Yes)**: Google Search grounding lets the model decide to search and answer with post-cutoff information supported by verifiable sources.

**References**: [Optimizing LLM Accuracy](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy) · [Long context (Gemini API) › RAG vs. long context](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/long-context) · [Grounding with Google Search (Gemini API)](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/google-search)

questions.title: Ordering steps to improve knowledge-assistant accuracy
questions.prompt:
Improve an internal knowledge assistant following OpenAI's accuracy-optimization guide. Order these five steps according to their documented dependencies.

- (1) Run the evaluation set with a basic prompt to obtain a baseline score and incorrect-answer list.
- (2) Apply RAG to knowledge-gap categories, distinguishing and fixing retrieval versus generation failures.
- (3) Classify incorrect answers as context/knowledge gaps or behavior/consistency problems.
- (4) Create an evaluation set with at least 20 question-answer pairs.
- (5) Remeasure with the same set and compare against baseline.

items.text: Run the evaluation set with a basic prompt to obtain a baseline score and incorrect-answer list.
Apply RAG to knowledge-gap categories, distinguishing and fixing retrieval versus generation failures.
Classify incorrect answers as context/knowledge gaps or behavior/consistency problems.
Create an evaluation set with at least 20 question-answer pairs.
Remeasure with the same set and compare against baseline.

questions.explanation:
| Order | Step | Dependency | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (4) Build evaluation set | None; establishes the artifact for every later measurement. | The guide recommends at least 20 question-answer pairs for a good baseline. |
| 2 | (1) Measure baseline | Requires the set to produce a score and incorrect answers. | The set plus basic prompt is the starting point. |
| 3 | (3) Classify failures | Uses incorrect answers produced by (1). | First diagnose each failure as context or behavior. |
| 4 | (2) Apply RAG and separate failure causes | Classification in (3) identifies where RAG fits. | Context optimization addresses missing knowledge. |
| 5 | (5) Remeasure | Requires the improved system and the same set from (4). | Comparing the same set reveals improvement. |

Additional note: The guide recommends maximizing accuracy with basic techniques before RAG or tuning.

**References**: [Optimizing LLM Accuracy](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy)

questions.title: Limits and remedies when entire documents are placed in context
questions.prompt:
A legal assistant inserts an entire roughly 700,000-token contract collection into every request. Many questions require finding several clauses together, such as termination conditions, penalties, and renewal deadlines. Requirements:

- Answers must be **grounded in original clauses**.
- Hundreds of daily queries over the same contracts create a substantial **input-cost burden**.
- **Accuracy loss from omitted items is unacceptable**.

Select **2** limitations/remedies consistent with Gemini's long-context documentation.

options.text: Multi-item retrieval can be less accurate than finding one item, so evaluate using real questions.
Use context caching to reduce repeated-input costs and place questions after the documents.
Since the contracts fit the context window, launch without separate per-item accuracy evaluation.
Send a separate request per item, retransmitting the entire collection without caching to maximize per-item accuracy.
Replace the contracts with summaries and omit originals from query context to reduce input costs.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are no omission-related accuracy loss and lower input costs. Gemini says needle-in-a-haystack single-item retrieval is only the simplest test. Finding multiple items can reduce accuracy and varies substantially with context. Repeated queries over the same documents benefit from context caching, and putting the question last generally improves long-context performance.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Acknowledge the limitation and test actual question types, as recommended.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Caching reduces repeated-query cost; question placement follows guidance.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Fitting the window does not guarantee accurate multi-item retrieval; this skips evaluation of a mandatory requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Separate item requests may improve accuracy but repeatedly resend the same document, maximizing input costs. Documentation identifies paying for input on every request as a drawback.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Summaries cannot guarantee original-clause grounding, and omitted clauses become unretrievable.

**References**: [Long context (Gemini API) › Long context limitations, Context caching, Best practices](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/long-context)

questions.title: A summarization service receiving 429s despite low token utilization
questions.prompt:
An OpenAI Responses API product-review summary service receives 429s at peaks. Requests are short—about 200 input and 60 output tokens—but numerous. Peak TPM utilization is only around 30%. Lowering `max_tokens` did not reduce 429s. Conditions:

- Users wait at their screens, so **preserve real-time responses**.
- **No tier upgrade this quarter**.
- Individual review summaries are **independent**.
- Maximum user wait is **three seconds**.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Lower `max_tokens` further to reduce estimated tokens per response, checking summary quality with evaluations.
Inspect remaining-request/token response headers to identify the bottleneck; if requests are limiting, bundle multiple reviews into each request.
Increase retry counts and shorten retry intervals to absorb temporary over-limit periods.
Move summaries to Batch API’s separate pool and update the screen when results become available.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are 30% TPM utilization and real-time responses. OpenAI limits apply when any metric, including RPM or TPM, reaches its cap first. Numerous short requests can exhaust request limits despite token headroom. `x-ratelimit-remaining-requests` and `x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens` identify the bottleneck. Documentation recommends bundling tasks when RPM is exhausted but TPM remains; independent items permit this.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; appropriate to another situation)**: `max_tokens` affects token-based usage estimates, not the likely request-count bottleneck at 30% TPM.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Diagnose first, then reduce request count, preserving real-time service without an upgrade. Tradeoffs are batching implementation changes and per-item error handling.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Failed requests also consume per-minute limits; more retries worsen congestion and short-interval retries can exceed the three-second deadline.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Batch legitimately uses separate limits, but asynchronous processing violates real-time requirements.

**References**: [Rate limits › Rate limit metrics, Response headers, Retry and backoff, Avoiding 429s](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/rate-limits)

questions.title: A 429 fallback needs a separate rate-limit pool
questions.prompt:
A Claude API contract-review service frequently receives 429s on Claude Fable 5.1 during peaks. It needs automatic fallback. Conditions:

- Fallback must work **independently of Fable 5.1's exhausted limit**.
- Its outputs must **pass task-specific quality evaluations in advance**.
- Failed requests must be processed **immediately, without waiting**.
- No additional contracts or organizations.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Fallback to the previous Fable 5 model and validate its outputs beforehand.
Fallback to Opus 5.5, checking its quality on production traffic when real 429s first occur.
Wait for `retry-after` and retry the same model without fallback; separately request a limit increase.
Fallback to Opus 5.5 after confirming it passes the task evaluation set in advance.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are independent limits and prior quality validation. Claude documentation says some models share pools: Fable 5.1 and Fable 5 share one, while Opus 5.5 and Opus 5 each have separate limits. Falling back within a shared pool continues consuming the same exhausted limit and does not solve the 429.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Prior evaluation is present, but Fable 5 and 5.1 share limits.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: The pool is separate, but production-only quality checks violate advance validation.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Waiting/retrying is standard handling but violates immediate service; a limit increase is not an immediate remedy.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: A separately limited, prevalidated model meets all conditions. Tradeoffs are different fallback pricing/quality and maintaining its evaluation set.

**References**: [Rate limits (Claude) › Shared model pools, Handling 429 errors](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits)

questions.title: Submitting 350,000 overnight requests through Message Batches
questions.prompt:
A Claude API team plans about 350,000 nightly document classifications through Message Batches. Its Build tier allows 300,000 queued batch requests simultaneously. Conditions:

- Results needed **the following morning**.
- Retain **half-price Batch discounts**.
- Do not affect **synchronous limits used by real-time services** in the same organization.
- Results must be stored **one-to-one per item**, so multiple items cannot share a request.

Which submission strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Split below the 100,000-request per-batch cap and submit later batches as earlier processing frees queue capacity.
Submit four batches simultaneously—three of 100,000 and one of 50,000—for maximum parallelism.
Use throttled synchronous Messages calls overnight, concentrating them during quiet hours to avoid contention.
Bundle three items per request, reducing the total to about 117,000 requests, and submit two batches simultaneously.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are the 300,000-request queue and one-to-one item storage. Message Batches permits up to 100,000 requests or 256MB per batch, whichever comes first. Tier queue limits count requests not yet processed. Split within batch limits and submit more as the queue shrinks to process all 350,000 while preserving discounts and synchronous-limit isolation.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It meets batch/queue limits, retains discounts, and avoids synchronous capacity. Tradeoffs are submission orchestration and potentially later overall completion.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Each batch fits, but simultaneous submission places 350,000 in a 300,000 queue.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Synchronous calls lose Batch discounts and consume limits shared with real-time services.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Queue size fits, but bundling violates one-to-one per-item requests/results.

**References**: [Batch processing (Claude) › Batch limitations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing) · [Rate limits (Claude) › Message Batches API limits](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits)

questions.title: Timing prewarming to avoid morning cache misses
questions.prompt:
An internal assistant uses GPT-5.6-or-later models. First requests just after 9 a.m. are slow due to cache misses. All employees share a 4,000-token system prompt, with no overnight user calls. Conditions:

- Reduce **latency immediately after 9 a.m.**
- **Avoid unnecessary overnight calls**, minimizing cache-write costs and operations.
- **All employees must share the cache** for the common prompt.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Send one prewarm request at 6 a.m. to cache the shared prompt before work.
Send prewarm requests every 25 minutes from midnight so the cache never expires overnight.
Send one prewarm request a few minutes before work begins, then disable prewarm on actual user requests.
Assign a different `prompt_cache_key` to each employee so each first request creates its own reusable cache.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are first-request latency after 9 a.m. and minimal unnecessary overnight calls. GPT-5.6-or-later prompt caches remain valid for at least 30 minutes after the last write/reuse; `prompt_cache_options.ttl` supports only `30m`. `prewarm: true` fills cache without output, billed at normal cache-write rates. One fill immediately before work is therefore the minimum sufficient approach.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: A minimum 30-minute lifetime does not guarantee a cache warmed three hours earlier survives until 9 a.m.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Reuse extends lifetime, but repeated overnight calls violate minimal unnecessary activity.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: One timely fill reduces latency at minimum cost. The tradeoff is a scheduled job aligned with the start of work.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: `prompt_cache_key` optionally separates customer/user cache accounting on GPT-5.6-or-later models. Employee-specific keys give everyone an initial miss instead of a shared cache.

**References**: [Prompt caching (OpenAI) › prompt\_cache\_options, prewarm, Cache price multipliers](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)

questions.title: Operating sequence for an overnight Batch pipeline
questions.prompt:
An overnight classification pipeline uses the OpenAI Batch API. Arrange the five steps according to their documented dependencies.

- (1) Create a batch with `input_file_id` and a `completion_window` of 24h.
- (2) Match results to inputs using `custom_id`, and resubmit only requests marked `batch_expired` in the error file in a new batch.
- (3) Create a JSONL input file with a unique `custom_id` for every request and requests for only one model per file.
- (4) Once the batch reaches a terminal state, download the output and error files.
- (5) Upload the input file with `purpose="batch"` and receive its file ID.

items.text: Create a batch with `input_file_id` and a `completion_window` of 24h.
Match results to inputs using `custom_id`, and resubmit only requests marked `batch_expired` in the error file in a new batch.
Create a JSONL input file with a unique `custom_id` for every request and requests for only one model per file.
Once the batch reaches a terminal state, download the output and error files.
Upload the input file with `purpose="batch"` and receive its file ID.

questions.explanation:
| Order | Step | Dependency on the previous step | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (3) Create JSONL | None. This creates the input file used by subsequent steps. | Input is JSONL with one request per line, a unique `custom_id`, and only one model per file. |
| 2 | (5) Upload | The file to upload must have been created in (3). | Upload it through the Files API with `purpose="batch"`. |
| 3 | (1) Create the batch | The creation request takes the file ID returned in (5). | Create it with `input_file_id`, an endpoint, and a `24h` window. |
| 4 | (4) Retrieve results | Output and error file IDs are finalized when the batch ends. | Results are in `output_file_id`; failures are in `error_file_id`. |
| 5 | (2) Match and resubmit | Matching unordered results by `custom_id` requires the files from (4). | Requests unfinished within the window are recorded as `batch_expired` in the error file. |

Also note: Output files are automatically deleted 30 days after batch completion. Even for an expired batch, completed responses remain in the output file, and their tokens are billed.

**References**: [Batch API (OpenAI) › Batch input, Creating a batch, Getting results, Expiration](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch)

questions.title: Meeting a weekend labeling deadline with Gemini Batch
questions.prompt:
A paid Gemini API project must finish a labeling workload of approximately 40 million tokens, finalized on Friday evening, by Monday at 8 a.m. AI Studio shows a Batch queued-token limit of 15 million tokens for this project's model and tier. The requirements are:

- Results are needed **by Monday at 8 a.m.**
- The **50% Batch discount must be retained**.
- The **queued-token limit must not be exceeded**.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Submit all 40 million tokens as one job and review the completed results together on Monday morning.
Submit jobs below the limit sequentially, but defer requests that fail after completion to the following week's batch.
Split the workload into jobs below the limit, continue submitting as the queue shrinks, check failure counts, and resubmit only failed requests in new jobs.
Send synchronous requests throughout the weekend within throughput limits to finish every request by Monday morning.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [queued-token limit] and [by Monday at 8 a.m.]. Gemini Batch queued-token limits depend on the model and tier and must be checked in AI Studio. Jobs are designed to target completion within 24 hours; jobs queued or running for more than 48 hours expire without results. After completion, `failedRequestCount` in `batchStats` reports the number of failures. With approximately 60 hours available, successive jobs below the limit are appropriate.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: 40 million tokens exceeds the [queued-token limit] of 15 million.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It respects the limit and discount, but postponing failures until next week prevents delivery of all results [by Monday at 8 a.m.].
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Successive jobs within the limit and immediate resubmission of failures satisfy all three requirements. The tradeoff is orchestration that monitors job states and continues submitting work.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Synchronous calls do not receive the Batch discount, violating [retain the 50% discount].

**References**: [Batch API (Gemini API) › Batch Mode, Expiration, Limits](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/batch-api) · [Rate limits (Gemini API) › Batch API rate limits](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits)

questions.title: Combining Message Batches and prompt caching overnight
questions.prompt:
Approximately 200,000 documents are classified overnight using Claude API Message Batches. Every request starts with the same 12,000-token block of classification instructions and examples. The requirements are:

- Results are reviewed the following morning, and **caching must maximize cost savings in addition to the Batch discount**.
- Requests are processed **concurrently** within the batch, so the team accepts that cache hits are not guaranteed.

Choose **two** configurations that reduce cost.

options.text: Because cache hits are not guaranteed, omit prompt caching and keep operations simple with only the Batch discount.
Use the default five-minute cache and submit separate batches at spaced intervals to distribute the cache-writing load.
Apply identical `cache_control` settings to the shared context blocks in every request so that the same prefix is cached.
Put each request's processing timestamp and request number at the beginning of the shared instructions to make results easier to trace later.
Because batches may take more than five minutes, use a one-hour cache for the shared context and submit requests in a steady, uninterrupted flow.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [caching savings in addition to the Batch discount] and [concurrent processing without guaranteed hits]. Claude documentation says Batch discounts and prompt caching stack, while concurrent request processing makes cache hits best-effort, typically 30–98%. To improve hit rates, it recommends identical `cache_control` blocks in every request, steady request flow to prevent entries from expiring, maximally identical shared context, and a one-hour cache because batches may take longer than five minutes.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Hits are indeed best-effort, but abandoning caching gives up stacked discounts and violates [maximize cost savings].
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: A five-minute cache can expire between spaced submissions and fail to be reused. This is the opposite of the documented recommendation for steady request flow.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Cache reuse requires an identical prefix, so identical block settings are fundamental.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Different values at the beginning of the prefix change its hash and prevent cache reuse. Use `custom_id` for request tracking.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: A one-hour cache and steady submissions account for batch processing duration and follow the recommendation. The tradeoff is that one-hour cache writes cost more than five-minute cache writes.

**References**: [Batch processing (Claude) › Using prompt caching with Message Batches](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing) · [Prompt caching (Claude) › Cache TTL, What invalidates the cache](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)

questions.title: Routing reasoning effort by difficulty while retaining the prompt cache
questions.prompt:
A support agent uses the OpenAI Responses API with a GPT-6-or-later model that supports mid-conversation configuration updates. Its long, multi-turn conversations repeat approximately 8,000 tokens of system instructions and tool definitions at the beginning. After the team began classifying each turn's difficulty and changing `reasoning.effort`, the prompt cache hit rate fell. The requirements are:

- Easy turns must use lower reasoning effort to **reduce cost and latency**.
- The **benefit of cache-read pricing** must be retained.
- Application changes must be **minimal**.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Keep top-level `reasoning.effort` fixed and append the difficulty decision as a `configuration_update` item at the end of the input to change effort.
Fix `reasoning.effort` at High for every turn to preserve the prefix and cache, and reduce cost through call-volume management and request limits.
Give up cache benefits and change top-level `reasoning.effort` for each request according to the turn's difficulty.
Whenever effort changes, summarize the previous conversation into a new prompt and send that summarized conversation as input.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [reduce cost and latency] and [retain cache-read pricing]. OpenAI's prompt caching documentation explains that changing top-level `reasoning.effort` changes hidden model instructions and breaks prefix reuse. Supported GPT-6-or-later models allow an appended `configuration_update` input item to change effort for subsequent responses while leaving the top-level value unchanged. The latest update applies to subsequent responses.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: It changes effort per turn while preserving the prefix, satisfying all three requirements. The tradeoffs are the supported-model limitation and maintaining a difficulty classifier.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It preserves caching, but using High even for easy turns gives up [reduce cost and latency].
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Although simplest to implement, it breaks prefix reuse and violates [retain cache-read pricing].
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: The documentation warns that summarization or truncation can reset reuse. Adding summarization logic also violates [minimal application changes].

**References**: [Prompt caching (OpenAI) › Reasoning effort and the prefix, Cache lifetime](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)

questions.title: Matching processing approaches to traffic patterns

| 4. A chatbot needs lower input costs, and every request starts with the same 6,000-token instructions. | d. Prompt caching |
| 5. Moving all traffic to a replacement model in one day risks exceeding limits and Priority downgrades. | e. Gradual rollout and jittered retries |
| | f. Lower `max_output_tokens` |

options.text: Batch API processing
Flex processing
Priority processing
Prompt caching
Gradual rollout and jittered retries
Lower `max_output_tokens`

items.text: Hundreds of thousands of documents are classified nightly; results are needed the following morning and asynchronous delivery is acceptable.

It also does not address pattern 4's input-cost problem. |

Also note: Gemini API pricing documentation also lists Batch, Flex, and Priority tiers, but this question matches approaches using OpenAI documentation only.
