questions.title: Isolating customers in a document assistant with a shared index
questions.prompt:
Hanbit Cloud is building a RAG-based SaaS document assistant shared by 40 customer organizations. Its index contains three million chunks. Even within one customer, document access differs by department (permission group). Requirements:

- **Other customers' documents must never appear in search results.**
- Within a customer, retrieve only documents allowed by the user's permission groups.
- With only three operators, retain a single search cluster.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Write "Do not use documents belonging to other customers or documents without permission" in the system instructions, but search the entire index.
Have the frontend submit customer-ID and permission-group filters, and have the search service apply them unchanged.
Store customer IDs and allowed permission groups as chunk metadata. Have the search service derive the customer and groups from the authenticated user token and enforce these filters on every query.
Create a separate index per user and copy all documents that user can access into it.

questions.explanation:
In shared multitenant infrastructure, isolation requires obtaining the requester identity from server-verified authentication and enforcing retrieval scope from that identity. Using customer IDs and allowed groups in document metadata is metadata filtering. Deriving those filters from user permissions and applying them to every query is ACL-aware retrieval. Neither model instructions nor client-supplied values constitute access control. The decisive constraints are [must never appear] and [one cluster].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Instructions guide model behavior but cannot prevent other customers' documents from being retrieved into model context, violating [must never appear].
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Clients can manipulate filter values to submit another customer's ID. Isolation criteria must come from server-verified identity.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: The server enforces isolation at retrieval time while maintaining one index and meeting the [one cluster] requirement. The tradeoff is attaching complete customer and permission metadata during ingestion and updating it when permissions change.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, excessive design)**: It isolates users but duplicates documents per user, increasing storage and update burdens. Maintaining consistency after revocations or edits is difficult for three operators.

Additional note: Filtering after retrieval can be safe, but may leave no results when most top candidates are removed. Prefer applying conditions during retrieval where possible. See Q36 for immediately blocking revoked documents.

**References**: General knowledge (multitenant isolation and server-enforced access control).

questions.title: Which synchronization design best meets requirements 1, 3, and 4?
questions.prompt: Which synchronization design best meets requirements 1, 3, and 4?
questions.context:
[Company overview] Haneul Precision manufactures industrial equipment. It operates a RAG technical-document assistant for maintenance technicians. Originals reside in an internal document management system (DMS); the assistant's vector index is derived from them.

[Existing environment]

- Approximately 80,000 documents; about 300 creations or updates and 30 deletions daily.
- The DMS provides a feed of changes since the last cursor. Deletions arrive as tombstone events, {doc_id, deleted: true}. A cursor remains valid for seven days after the last call and then produces an error.
- Reading and embedding all documents again takes about nine hours and is expensive.
- The indexer currently processes only creation and update events. There are two operators.

[Requirements]

1. Document edits must become searchable within 30 minutes.
2. Deleted documents must disappear from results within one hour.
3. Minimize embedding costs.
4. Inconsistencies from feed failures or omissions must not accumulate.

options.text: Perform a full sync every 30 minutes, rereading and re-embedding every DMS document.

Perform an initial backfill once, then apply only changes from the feed cursor every 30 minutes (delta sync). Each night, reconcile DMS document IDs and modification times against the index and repair omissions. Fall back to a full sync if the cursor expires.
Perform an initial backfill, then assume the feed is complete and operate only a delta sync every 30 minutes.
Run one full sync each night and make no updates during the day.

questions.explanation:
Initial backfill fills the entire dataset once. Delta sync applies only changes identified by a feed or modification times. Full sync rereads everything. Reconciliation compares source and index inventories to repair differences missed by delta updates. The decisive details are [30 minutes] in requirement 1, [minimize cost] in requirement 3, [prevent accumulated inconsistencies] in requirement 4, and [cursor expires after seven days].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, excessive design)**: A nine-hour re-embedding job cannot meet a 30-minute interval and costs far too much for 300 daily changes, violating requirements 1 and 3.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Delta sync provides timely updates at lower cost. Nightly inventory reconciliation catches omissions without re-embedding everything. Full sync recovers from cursor expiration and supports requirement 4. The tradeoff is operating reconciliation and a recovery path.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Failed feed calls or expired cursors leave missed changes accumulating. Without reconciliation it violates requirement 4.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Daytime edits wait for the next nightly run, missing requirement 1's 30-minute target, even if costs fall.

Additional note: Reconciliation is inexpensive because it compares IDs and modification times or hashes without re-embedding document bodies.

**References**: General knowledge (initial backfill, incremental synchronization, and reconciliation patterns).

questions.title: Which improvement meets requirement 2 and correctly monitors freshness?
questions.prompt:
Which improvement meets requirement 2 and correctly monitors freshness?

Technicians report that the assistant still cites procedures withdrawn last week. Investigation finds that the indexer skips deleted: true events. The operations dashboard currently displays only the indexing-job success rate.
questions.context:
[Company overview] Haneul Precision manufactures industrial equipment. It operates a RAG technical-document assistant for maintenance technicians. Originals reside in an internal document management system (DMS); the assistant's vector index is derived from them.

[Existing environment]

- Approximately 80,000 documents; about 300 creations or updates and 30 deletions daily.
- The DMS provides a feed of changes since the last cursor. Deletions arrive as tombstone events, {doc_id, deleted: true}. A cursor remains valid for seven days after the last call and then produces an error.
- Reading and embedding all documents again takes about nine hours and is expensive.
- The indexer currently processes only creation and update events. There are two operators.

[Requirements]

1. Document edits must become searchable within 30 minutes.
2. Deleted documents must disappear from results within one hour.
3. Minimize embedding costs.
4. Inconsistencies from feed failures or omissions must not accumulate.

options.text: On a tombstone event, delete all chunks and embeddings for its doc_id from the index idempotently. Measure the 95th-percentile lag from source change to searchable update and compare it against the 30-minute update and one-hour deletion targets.
Delete the document's chunks on a tombstone event, but continue monitoring freshness using the indexing-job success rate.
Leave the indexer unchanged and rely on nightly full sync to remove chunks for documents no longer in the DMS.
Add "Do not cite withdrawn procedures" to the answer-generation instructions and leave the index unchanged.

questions.explanation:
Delta sync propagates deletions through separate tombstone events that the indexer must process. Data freshness measures the lag from a source change until that change is reflected in retrieval; measuring it makes comparison with a target possible. Job success and update speed are different metrics. The decisive details are [skipped deleted: true events], [success rate only], and requirement 2's [one hour].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Handling tombstones directly fixes the cause and latency percentiles monitor freshness. Idempotent deletion makes repeated delivery safe.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Deletion handling is correct, but success rate only indicates whether a job finished without failure, not how many minutes an update took. It cannot monitor freshness targets.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Nightly deletion can leave documents searchable for nearly a day, violating the one-hour target. Nightly reconciliation is a repair mechanism, not the primary deletion path.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, remedy for another situation)**: The model cannot know which documents were withdrawn, and instructions do not prevent them entering context.

Additional note: Search filters can supplement tombstones when immediate blocking is required, such as permission revocations (see Q36).

**References**: General knowledge (deletion propagation in incremental sync and data-freshness metrics).

questions.title: Ingesting documents duplicated across folders
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics wants to ingest 120,000 documents into an internal search RAG system. Contract PDFs are copied into departmental folders, making approximately 35% identical copies. Chunking and embedding every copy fills the top five results with duplicate content and increases embedding costs and storage. Requirements:

- Reduce embedding costs and storage.
- Departments control the source system, so **copies cannot be deleted or moved**.
- A user allowed to access any folder containing a copy must be able to view the document.

Which ingestion-pipeline approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Ingest everything as before, then deduplicate identical chunks in search results before passing them to the model.
Ask each department to keep only the latest-modified copy and delete the others from the source system.
Increase top-k from 10 to 30 so the model receives evidence beyond the duplicate copies.
Deduplicate during ingestion using normalized-body hashes, chunking and embedding content once. Aggregate copy locations and permissions in metadata and authorize access using their union.

questions.explanation:
Deduplication during ingestion avoids unnecessary embedding and storage. Hashes of normalized bodies identify exactly identical documents. Because copies have different location-based permissions, preserve their locations and permissions in aggregated metadata rather than discarding them. The decisive constraints are [lower cost and storage], [cannot delete or move copies], and [access through any authorized folder].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, remedy for another situation)**: Result diversity improves, but retrieval-time deduplication does not undo embedding costs or storage already incurred. The cost-and-storage requirement calls for ingestion-time processing.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Deleting source copies violates the explicit constraint and may remove access for users of those folders.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Duplicates still occupy candidates while increasing model input tokens. Embedding costs and storage remain unchanged.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: Embedding once reduces cost and storage. Aggregating permissions across all locations preserves access through any authorized copy. The tradeoff is updating the location list as copies are added or removed.

Additional note: Hashes detect exact content equality. Slightly different revisions are separate versions, not duplicates; distinguish them with version and effective-date metadata.

**References**: General knowledge (content-hash deduplication in ingestion pipelines).

questions.title: Matching reliability terminology
questions.prompt: Match each of five descriptions from an LLM customer-support team's documentation to the most appropriate term. One option is unused.

options.text: SLI
SLO
SLA
Uptime
RTO
RPO

items.text: The proportion of a month during which the service could process requests normally.
The measured proportion of requests whose first response starts within three seconds, calculated every five minutes and shown on a dashboard.
The team's internal goal to keep that proportion at or above 99% each month.
A customer-contract promise to refund part of the fee if monthly uptime falls below 99.5%.
The maximum time allowed after an outage before the service becomes usable again.

questions.explanation:
An SLI measures service level; an SLO is an internal target for that measure; an SLA is a contractual commitment with consequences such as compensation for failure. Uptime is the proportion of time the service operates normally. RTO and RPO describe the maximum acceptable recovery time and data-loss window, respectively.

| Item | Answer | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | {{option:d}} | The proportion of time operating normally is uptime. |
| 2 | {{option:a}} | A defined measurement of what and how to measure is an SLI. |
| 3 | {{option:b}} | An internal target for the measurement is an SLO. |
| 4 | {{option:c}} | A customer contract with refunds for failure is an SLA. |
| 5 | {{option:e}} | The upper limit on recovery time is RTO. |
| Unused | {{option:f}} | RPO concerns the allowable data-loss time window; none of these descriptions addresses it. |

Additional note: Internal SLOs are generally stricter than SLAs. The team should detect and respond to SLO breaches before they become SLA violations and compensation obligations.

**References**: General knowledge (SLI/SLO/SLA in SRE and RTO/RPO in disaster recovery).

questions.title: Good average latency but complaints from a few users
questions.prompt: Nuri Insurance's internal translation assistant averages 2.1 seconds per response, meeting its three-second target and showing green on the dashboard. Users nevertheless report occasional waits exceeding 15 seconds. Logs show about 1% of requests exceed 15 seconds, mostly long documents or requests queued during peaks. Select TWO appropriate improvements.

options.text: Define p95/p99 latency as SLIs rather than the average, segment requests by characteristics such as input length, and set targets accordingly.
Because the average meets the target, consider the system healthy and treat slow cases as individual users' network issues.
Increase concurrent requests without limit: higher throughput will also reduce slow requests.
Break down p99 requests by input/output token lengths and queue wait; address long inputs or peak queues with input splitting or capacity/concurrency adjustments.
Switch the latency target to median (p50) to improve target attainment.

questions.explanation:
An average can hide a small number of very slow requests. User-visible tail latency requires percentiles such as p95 and p99, and component-level analysis explains why those requests are slow. Throughput counts requests or tokens processed per time unit and is a separate dimension. The clues are [2.1-second average shown green], [1% over 15 seconds], and [long inputs and queues].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Directly measuring tail latency and segmenting request types reveals the problematic groups.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: A good average does not remove the 15-second experience of 1% of users. Blaming individual users misses structural causes.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, confusing related functions)**: Throughput and tail latency are different metrics. Unlimited concurrency can saturate queues and provider limits and worsen tail latency.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: Long inputs and queue waits require different remedies, so breaking down tail requests supports targeted fixes.
- **{{option:E}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: A median target hides the slowest 1% even more when most requests are fast. It makes the target easier without improving experience.

Additional note: p99 is volatile with few requests; aggregate over a period with sufficient samples.

**References**: General knowledge (latency percentiles and the distinction between throughput and latency).

questions.title: Meeting vector-index disaster-recovery objectives
questions.prompt:
Haneul Precision's knowledge assistant keeps source documents in a repository and derives a vector index from them. The source repository and change-event log are already replicated to another region. Rebuilding the index, including embeddings, takes about 11 hours; restoring an index snapshot takes about 90 minutes. Requirements:

- Resume search **within four hours** of a regional outage (RTO four hours).
- Reflect document changes immediately preceding the outage after recovery (RPO within one hour).
- There is no budget to serve actively from two regions at all times.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Use only high availability (HA), with index replicas across availability zones in the same region.
Document a procedure to rebuild the index from scratch after failure and rehearse quarterly.
Operate active-active indexes serving continuously from two regions.
Copy an index snapshot to another region daily. After failure, restore it and replay subsequent change events. Verify recovery time through regular rehearsals.

questions.explanation:
RTO is the allowed recovery time; RPO is the acceptable data-loss window. High availability (HA) tolerates component or availability-zone failures. Disaster recovery (DR) restores service after larger incidents such as regional failures or data corruption. Here the index is derived from protected sources, allowing snapshot restoration plus change replay. The clues are [regional outage], [11 hours versus 90 minutes], [four-hour RTO and one-hour RPO], and [no active-active budget].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, remedy for another situation)**: It handles availability-zone failures, not a regional outage. Same-region replicas also reproduce erroneous deletions.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: An 11-hour rebuild violates the four-hour RTO; rehearsing alone does not shorten that duration.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, excessive design)**: It meets recovery goals but violates the budget constraint and exceeds what a four-hour recovery target requires.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: The intended design restores in 90 minutes and replays changes within the remaining recovery window. Protected change logs recover changes since the snapshot and support the RPO. The tradeoff is maintaining snapshot copies and restoration drills.

Additional note: Protecting source data and change logs, rather than the index alone, is key to the RPO. Snapshot frequency affects replay duration and therefore RTO.

**References**: General knowledge (RTO/RPO and high availability versus disaster recovery).

questions.title: Output formatting drifts despite a pinned model ID
questions.prompt: Nuri Insurance summarizes claim documents with the Claude API model ID claude-sonnet-5-5. Prompts and parameters are versioned and have not changed for a month. Since last week, slight differences in JSON key order and whitespace have intermittently broken a downstream system that parses through string comparison. Team policy permits production model or prompt changes only after regression evaluation. Which interpretation and response best match Anthropic's documentation?

options.text: The documentation says the model weights and configuration referenced by an ID do not change, but infrastructure updates may subtly affect observed behavior. Version the model ID, prompt, and parameters as one release; run regular formatting regression evaluations and make downstream parsing tolerant of formatting differences.
Pinning an ID guarantees identical behavior forever, so assume the prompt is responsible and keep editing it.
Unpin the version and automatically adopt every new ID in the model family, hoping the latest model fixes formatting.
Having observed a formatting change, immediately switch to an older-generation model ID without evaluation.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's documentation says each model ID references a fixed version: the underlying model stays unchanged for that ID's lifetime, and model or configuration changes receive new IDs. It also notes that infrastructure updates can cause subtle differences in observed behavior even with identical IDs and weights, and identifies infrastructure updates as the most likely cause of unexpected changes. Pinning is necessary for change control, but does not promise forever-identical behavior. Version the model ID, prompt, and parameters together and monitor with regression tests. The decisive details are [unchanged prompts and parameters] and [only after regression evaluation].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: It respects both the meaning and limits of pinning, follows evaluation policy, and fixes brittle formatting dependence.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, factual error)**: The guarantee concerns the underlying model referenced by an ID, not permanently identical observed behavior. Infrastructure updates may introduce subtle differences.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: It changes production before evaluation, violating policy, without guaranteeing a formatting fix.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Changing models without investigation or evaluation violates the same policy and may introduce other regressions.

Additional note: Each model ID has its own retirement schedule, which must be tracked (see Q17 and Q18).

**References**: [Model IDs and versioning (Claude API)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/model-ids-and-versions) · The supplied source identifies claude-sonnet-5-5 using the API ID in Models overview(https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview) and applies the linked page's rule that dateless IDs from generation 4.6 onward are fixed snapshots. · General knowledge (regression testing).

questions.title: Changing an internal classification API response format
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics' platform team operates an LLM document-classification API used by 12 teams. Responses currently look like {"category": "invoice"}. Documents must now support multiple classifications, requiring a categories array. Consumer teams have deployment schedules differing by four to eight weeks, and some branch downstream logic on category. Requirements:

- **Consumer services must not be interrupted.**
- The platform team will not maintain both formats forever.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Replace category with a categories array, deploy it, and announce the change internally.
Force all 12 teams to deploy on the same day and switch simultaneously.
Add categories while retaining category for backward compatibility. Announce a removal date and migration instructions, and remove category after confirming all consumers have migrated.
Expose the new format only through a separate v2 endpoint and retain v1 forever regardless of consumers' circumstances.

questions.explanation:
A change is backward compatible when existing consumers continue working without modification. Renaming, changing the type of, or removing fields can be a breaking change. Transition by adding a field, running both during migration, and announcing removal. The clues are [four-to-eight-week schedule differences], [no service interruption], and [not maintained forever].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Changing both name and type immediately breaks consumers relying on category. An announcement alone cannot prevent outages.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: A simultaneous switch is unrealistic given the schedule differences; any team that misses it may experience interruption.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: The new field leaves existing consumers working. Teams migrate on their own schedules during overlap, with an eventual removal point. The tradeoff is managing both fields temporarily.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Keeping v1 forever contradicts the requirement not to operate two formats indefinitely.

Additional note: The same principle applies to LLM output schemas. Changes to a model or prompt that alter output fields can be breaking changes for API consumers.

**References**: General knowledge (API versioning and backward compatibility).

questions.title: Using a beta feature in the critical path
questions.prompt: Hanbit Payments' support chatbot uses the Claude API. Developers find a cost-saving feature that requires naming it in the anthropic-beta request header. The service promises 99.9% monthly availability in its SLA. Internal policy prohibits mandatory critical-path dependencies on features not generally available (GA). Which approach best matches Anthropic's documentation?

options.text: Ban beta features entirely and do not reassess even after GA until the next annual review.

Keep the critical path functional with GA features alone. Test the beta behind a feature flag on limited traffic, automatically fall back to the GA configuration if it fails or is discontinued, and monitor cost and limit differences separately.
Deploy the beta to all traffic and roll back only if a problem occurs.
Treat the date suffix in its name as a guaranteed stability deadline and use it for all traffic until then.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic describes beta features as experimental functionality available before inclusion in the standard API. Betas may undergo announced breaking changes, be discontinued or removed, have different rate limits or prices, or be unavailable in some regions. The date suffix indicates the beta release date. Treat beta as an isolated experiment with a GA fallback, not a mandatory dependency for an SLA-backed critical path. The decisive constraints are [99.9% SLA] and [no non-GA critical-path dependency].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, excessive response)**: This exceeds the policy's goal. Noncritical testing and reassessment after GA can still deliver cost savings.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: It preserves a GA critical path and evaluates savings through isolated testing and fallback. The tradeoff is maintaining two configurations.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Discontinuation or changes to limits or pricing affect the whole service and threaten the policy and SLA. Rollback after an incident does not prevent the violation.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, factual error)**: The suffix is the release date, not a guaranteed stability deadline.

Additional note: A nonexistent beta name or one unavailable to the organization produces a 400 error. Use the exact name in feature documentation.

**References**: [Beta headers (Claude API)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/beta-headers) · General knowledge (GA policies and fallback design).

questions.title: Reducing cost and latency for differently worded repeat questions
questions.prompt:
About 40% of questions to Nuri Insurance's HR assistant ask the same thing in different words, such as "Tell me the leave carryover rules" and "How do I carry over leave?" Prompt caching already covers 3,000 tokens of fixed instructions, but response-generation call counts and latency remain unchanged. Answers differ by job grade, and the policy manual changes quarterly. Requirements:

- Reduce model calls and response time.
- **Never return another grade's answer or an answer based on an outdated policy.**

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Use a semantic cache to reuse answers to highly similar question embeddings. Include job grade (permission group) and policy version in the cache key, set a high similarity threshold, and invalidate relevant entries on policy revisions.
Extend prompt-cache retention and enlarge the cached prefix so repeated questions read the same cache.
Use an exact-question-string hash cache, stored separately per job grade.
Lower the similarity threshold to maximize hit rate and use one global cache without grade separation.

questions.explanation:
Prompt caching reduces repeated-prefix processing cost and latency but still generates a response each time. Semantic caching is an application or gateway pattern that returns a previous response for similar meanings, avoiding the model call itself. It differs from provider prompt caching. Because responses are reused, cache keys must reflect whether the same answer remains valid for the same question. The clues are [40% reworded repeats], [unchanged call counts], and [grade- and revision-specific answers].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: It eliminates calls for equivalent questions while grade/version keys and invalidation prevent inappropriate reuse. A higher threshold reduces hit rate, and embedding/storage infrastructure must be operated.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, confusing related functions)**: Prefix reuse does not eliminate generation calls. Unchanged call counts despite existing prompt caching are the clue.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, remedy for another situation)**: Small wording differences miss the cache, losing most repeated questions. Exact-match caches suit nearly identical inputs.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Low thresholds and a global cache may return another grade's answer or answers to similar but different questions, violating the requirement.

Additional note: Avoid semantic caching responses containing personal or user-specific data, or isolate keys per user.

**References**: General knowledge (semantic caching and cache-key design). See Q09 and Q53 for the distinction from prompt caching.

questions.title: One customer's bulk upload blocks the shared summarization service
questions.prompt:
Hanbit's document-summarization SaaS calls an LLM provider API with a project-level per-minute limit. A customer uploading thousands of documents exhausts the limit, causing other customers' requests to receive 429 errors. Requests currently use synchronous HTTP, and bulk uploads hit the gateway's 60-second timeout. Requirements:

- Ensure fair usage across customers.
- Summaries may take a few minutes.
- Stay within provider limits and keep operations simple.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Improve only exponential-backoff retries on 429 and retain synchronous calls.
Greatly increase synchronous workers and extend the gateway timeout to ten minutes.

Enforce per-customer quotas and concurrency caps at the gateway. Queue requests and immediately return job IDs. Limit total worker-pool concurrency within provider limits, schedule customers fairly, and expose results by job ID.
Create a separate provider project and account for each customer to divide limits.

questions.explanation:
Provider rate limits are shared across customers. Quotas allocate usage shares, while concurrency limits bound simultaneous work. Jobs whose results may arrive within minutes fit asynchronous processing: enqueue a request and return a job ID. The clues are [one customer exhausts the limit], [60-second timeout], [a few minutes acceptable], and [must not exceed provider limits].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: Retries do not distinguish the customer consuming the limit from others, so they do not ensure fairness. Synchronous calls still hit the timeout.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: More workers concentrate provider calls and exhaust limits faster. Longer timeouts also hold connections and resources longer.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Quotas and concurrency caps support fairness, queueing and job IDs avoid the synchronous timeout, and bounded total concurrency reduces 429s. The tradeoff is maintaining the queue and job-status service.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, excessive design)**: Accounts, keys, and limit allocations multiply per customer. This is more burdensome than application-level allocation.

Additional note: Dequeue fairly across customers so one backlog does not block everyone else. See Q13 for provider-side workspace limits.

**References**: General knowledge (gateway quotas, concurrency control, and asynchronous job queues).

questions.title: Keeping both storage and inference within the United States
questions.prompt:
Nuri Medi provides medical-device document summaries to US hospitals using the Claude API (Claude Opus 5.5). Contract requirements:

- **Model inference must run only on US infrastructure.**
- Data must also be stored in the US.
- The security checklist includes encryption in transit and at rest.
- Minimize code changes.

The security team claims that TLS and at-rest encryption already satisfy location requirements. Which configuration best matches Anthropic's documentation?

options.text: Accept the security team's view and use the default global configuration without further settings because encryption is enabled.

Create a workspace with US workspace geo for storage and set inference_geo to "us", per request or as a workspace default. Keep encryption as a separate requirement and include the US-only inference premium of 1.1 times standard pricing.
Set only workspace geo to US; inference then automatically stays in the US with no further configuration.
Place the frontend proxy in a US-region VPC and assume model inference therefore also runs in the US.

questions.explanation:
Encryption at rest and in transit protect readability; they do not determine where data is stored (residency) or processed. Anthropic distinguishes two settings. inference_geo controls inference location per request or by workspace default: "global" is default and "us" restricts inference to US infrastructure. Workspace geo sets storage and endpoint-processing location when the workspace is created. US-only inference for Claude 4.6 and later is billed at 1.1 times standard pricing. The clues are [inference only on US infrastructure], [storage also in the US], and [the encryption claim].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, confusing related functions)**: Encryption and location are separate controls. "global" permits inference elsewhere and does not satisfy US-only inference.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: It configures storage and inference independently, preserves encryption requirements, and accounts for the surcharge. Code changes are limited to parameter configuration; the tradeoff is the 1.1-times cost.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, factual error)**: The settings are independent: workspace geo covers storage and endpoint processing; inference_geo governs inference.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, confusing related functions)**: Proxy location is part of the request path, not the location where the model executes inference.

Additional note: The documentation says workspace geo is fixed at creation and cannot subsequently change; at the question's reference date, only "us" is available. Sending inference_geo to older unsupported models produces a 400 error. See Q15 and Q65 for other providers' regional-processing settings.

**References**: [Data residency (Claude API)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/data-residency) · General knowledge (encryption at rest and in transit).

questions.title: Excluding abuse-monitoring content while retaining stored responses
questions.prompt:
Haneul Precision's legal team is building a contract-review assistant with OpenAI's Responses API. Requirements:

- **Customer content, including prompts and responses, must not be retained in OpenAI abuse-monitoring logs.**
- The product relies on OpenAI-stored response state for multi-turn conversations. There is no staff available to build a new conversation store.

Which security proposal is most appropriate?

options.text: Set store=false on every request, which also excludes content from abuse-monitoring logs.
Apply for and enable Zero Data Retention (ZDR) for the organization.
Enable Modified Abuse Monitoring (MAM) directly in project settings without approval.

Obtain OpenAI approval for Modified Abuse Monitoring and apply it to the project. Customer content is excluded from abuse-monitoring logs, while foreground requests with store omitted or true retain standard retention and stored-response functionality.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI's data-controls documentation says abuse-monitoring logs are generated by default for API features and retained for up to 30 days. Modified Abuse Monitoring excludes customer content from those logs. ZDR also excludes it but additionally treats store as false for Responses and Chat Completions. These controls require prior approval from OpenAI. Under MAM, foreground requests with store omitted or true follow standard retention. The decisive constraints are [no customer content in abuse-monitoring logs], [dependence on stored response state], and [no staff for a new store].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, confusing related functions)**: store controls application-state storage of responses, not abuse-monitoring logs. Those logs have separate default retention, and disabling response storage also breaks the required multi-turn design.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, constraint violation)**: ZDR forces store=false, preventing the stored-response design and requiring the conversation store that the team lacks staff to build.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, factual error)**: These controls require OpenAI's prior approval; they cannot simply be enabled unilaterally.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It excludes content from abuse-monitoring logs while preserving stored responses. The tradeoffs are approval lead time and continued standard retention for response state.

Additional note: Even under MAM or ZDR, endpoints ineligible for ZDR, such as files and conversations, may still store application state. See Q63 for project-level configuration. The documentation also notes rare exceptions for image and file inputs under MAM.

**References**: [Data controls in the OpenAI platform](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data) › Modified Abuse Monitoring, Zero Data Retention.

questions.title: Matching retrieval failures to remedies
questions.prompt: Match each of five RAG retrieval symptoms to the most appropriate remedy. One option is unused.

options.text: Hybrid retrieval that combines keyword search such as BM25 with embedding search.
Rerank candidates and pass only the top few to the model.
Metadata filtering that narrows retrieval using query conditions such as year and status.
ACL-aware retrieval with filters derived from the authenticated user's permissions and enforced server-side on every query.
Delta sync to reduce the delay in reflecting changes in the index.
Add "Use only the most exactly matching documents" to the system instructions.

items.text: An exact query for "ERR-5071" retrieves semantically similar errors but not the document containing that exact code.
The correct document appears among the first-stage top 150 candidates but not the top five sent to the model.
A query for "2026 revised leave policy" returns a policy abolished in 2019. Documents include year and active/abolished status metadata.
For the same question, documents outside a user's departmental access permissions must be excluded from candidates.
Documents change daily, but search still shows yesterday's content.

questions.explanation:
Embedding search is strong at semantic similarity but may miss exact strings. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval article recommends combining BM25 and embedding results. It also describes retrieving 150 candidates, reranking them to 20, and passing those to the model.

| Item | Answer | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | {{option:a}} | A missing exact error code calls for keyword matching alongside embeddings. |
| 2 | {{option:b}} | A relevant document present but ranked too low calls for reranking existing candidates. |
| 3 | {{option:c}} | Restricting by query conditions such as year and status is metadata filtering. |
| 4 | {{option:d}} | The filter comes from permissions rather than query conditions and must be server-enforced, so this is ACL-aware retrieval (see SDA-N1). |
| 5 | {{option:e}} | The index lags source changes, a freshness issue addressed with delta sync (see SDA-N2). |
| Unused | {{option:f}} | Instructions do not determine which documents enter retrieval results and solve none of these symptoms. |

Additional note: Items 3 and 4 both use filters, but item 3 derives values from user query conditions while item 4 derives them from server-verified identity. Client-submitted values must not control item 4's permissions.

**References**: [Introducing Contextual Retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval) · General knowledge (metadata filtering, ACL-aware retrieval, and incremental synchronization).
